verses.1:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse addresses idol worshipers alone, as its context continues to argue against them until “Your God is the One God… (16:22).” The coming edict is God’s promised judgment: it will purify His lordship of their polytheism and fulfill the warnings given to them, while vindicating His Messenger and the believers. In Qur’anic usage, those who impatiently demand the Hour, punishment, victory, or judgment are idolaters, not believers.

“Allah’s edict is coming!” may express the imminence of an event whose occurrence is certain, although it has not yet taken place. The pronoun in “do not seek to hasten it” refers to this edict. The shift from directly addressing them—“do not seek to hasten it”—to speaking of “any partners that they ascribe to Him” marks their contemptibility: their demand for punishment arises from polytheism and mocks the prophets’ summons.

The commentary therefore rejects the view that believers as well as idolaters are addressed. It also rejects identifying the edict specifically with the Day of Judgment: believers are described as apprehensive of it, whereas those without faith demand that it be hastened (42:18). Arguments based on verbal parallels with the end of Sūrah al-Ḥijr are tortuous and do not overcome the context. Equally flawed is the claim that amr means a legislative command disclosed in this sūrah and that the prohibition of haste is consequently directed to believers.
verses.2:
Al-Mizan explains rūh as that by which there is life marked by consciousness and will. The Qur’an presents the Spirit as an independent, living, knowing, and powerful reality, not a mere quality inhering in something else, since it distinguishes the Spirit from the angels. It is “of the command of my Lord” (17:85): the divine command is God’s creative word, the existence He bestows, free from materiality, time, space, and gradual motion. Thus the Spirit is God’s word of life, imparted to a prophet’s heart as revelation.

Whether bi in “with the Spirit of His command” denotes accompaniment or causation, the central meaning is alike: angels descend and the Spirit is instilled in the prophet’s heart, preparing it for divine knowledge; this life-giving command also affects the angels. The verse thereby explains why God is exalted above partners: He sends angels with a Spirit from His command to whom He wills, warning humanity that no god exists except Him and that they must be wary of Him.

The commentary rejects interpreting min amri-hi as “by His command.” Here min retains its sense of origin: the Spirit is from, and an aspect of, the divine command, as in “The Spirit is of the command of my Lord.” The interpretation of Spirit as revelation, the Qur’an, or prophethood captures a consequence—its descent results in revelation and prophethood—but does not identify what the Spirit itself is. Qur’anic terms must be explained through Qur’anic usage rather than a lexical metaphor that calls revelation “spirit” because it revives hearts.

The Spirit is a created reality with degrees: one level occurs in animals and unbelieving humans; a higher one strengthens believers; and another strengthens prophets and messengers, as in “and strengthened them with a spirit from Him (58:22),” “and supported him with the Holy Spirit (2:87),” and “Thus have We revealed to you the Spirit of Our dispensation (42:52).” Technical disputes over whether this use is literal, metaphorical, or simile do not uncover the intended truth.

Nor is the Spirit Gabriel. Though “the Trustworthy Spirit” in another context denotes Gabriel, “He casts the Spirit of His command upon whomever of His servants that He wishes, that he may warn of the Day of Encounter” (40:15) cannot plausibly mean that Gabriel is cast upon any chosen servant in this manner. The claim attributed to Mujāhid that it means human spirits is still less credible.

“To whomever He wishes of His servants” means that no one compels, obstructs, or overpowers God in sending messengers and bestowing this grace. Yet His will does not exclude wisdom or recipients’ preparedness: divine grace is bestowed in accordance with their capacity and suitability, without their capacity compelling Him. Thus God knows where to place messengership, and the dependence of prophethood on His will does not mean that prophets have no distinctive merit or readiness. Nor does it prove that prophethood, unlike acquired matters, alone comes without human effort, since every acquired matter also exists only by God’s permission.

The command to warn explains the descent of the angels and Spirit. Whether indhār means informing with fear or announcing danger, its content is God’s exclusive divinity and the consequent command to fear Him. The fa in “so be wary of Me” makes God-wariness follow from “there is no god except Me”: because all good and happiness depend on the sole deity, taqwā requires sound belief as well as rectified action. Prophetic warning therefore addresses both corrupted belief—summed up in denying God’s oneness—and corrupted practice—summed up in the call to be wary of Him; it is not confined to the Quraysh or merely to those who had sought punishment hastened.
verses.3:
Al-Mizan explains that the heavens and earth were created “in truth,” with no falsehood belonging to their creation. The alleged partners invoked for intercession, good, and protection are therefore falsehoods with no place in God’s dominion.

The verse and those following establish God’s exclusive divinity through creation and providence. Cosmic creation and its signs indicate divinity, while creatures’ benefits to one another disclose lordship: benefit presupposes connections forming a unified system, a unified system requires a unified governance, and unified governance indicates one Governor. Since all beings in heaven and earth benefit humanity within this order, God alone is the Lord of humanity and of all things.
verses.4: Al-Mizan takes human creation from seminal fluid as a statement of the ordinary process of human generation; Adam and Jesus are exceptions and do not contradict it. Khaṣīm means an argumentative contender. Although the verse could be read as recalling the favor by which a lowly drop becomes a rational, articulate human being, its context and comparable verses show that it chiefly reproaches human audacity: one created from an insignificant fluid shamelessly disputes with God and associates partners with Him.
verses.5: Al-Mizan explains anʿām as camels, cows, and sheep. Their difʾun is the warmth supplied by their skins and wool against cold, or possibly bodily heat; their other uses include milk, meat, hides, and similar benefits. “For you” may qualify their creation or specifically the warmth and benefits found in them.
verses.6: Al-Mizan explains that livestock have beauty both when they are driven to pasture at dawn and when they return from grazing at dusk. Turīḥūn denotes bringing a herd or flock home for its evening rest, while tasraḥūn denotes releasing it from its enclosure to graze in the morning.
verses.7: Al-Mizan explains athqāl as heavy burdens. Livestock such as camels and oxen carry people’s loads to towns that they could reach only through arduous exertion without them. By creating these animals and subjecting them to human use, God removes a hardship that people could scarcely bear, displaying His kindness and mercy.
verses.8: Al-Mizan connects horses, mules, and asses to the preceding cattle: God created them for people to ride and to regard as adornment, both being human benefits. “He creates what you do not know” refers to further creatures unknown to people, which He has subjected to them for their benefit.
verses.9:
Al-Mizan explains qaṣd al-sabīl as the directing, straight path that conveys its traveler to the goal, in contrast to jāʾir, which deviates from that goal. “With Allah rests guidance to the straight path” means that God has made it incumbent upon Himself to establish for His servants the way that leads to happiness and to Him. He does so by giving every being the faculties through which it can attain its proper perfection, and, for human beings, through fiṭra as well as messengers, scriptures, and laws. The verse occurs amid material blessings because physical journeys and riding animals suitably introduce the spiritual path of life.

God attributes the straight path to Himself but does not attribute the devious way to Himself, because misguidance is not an actual alternative path established by God; it is departure from the path. It neither leads to God nor has independent reality as a path. The clause “had He wished He would have guided you all” prevents the mistaken inference that people’s refusal of guidance defeats God: He could compel universal guidance, but the path He has set is one of free choice. Because people differ in their constitutions and dispositions, they differ in faith and unbelief, obedience and sin; such a freely chosen way cannot be compulsory or universal.

The Muʿtazilīs infer from the differing attribution of the two ways that some things may be attributed to God and others may not. Ashʿarī responses variously say that both ways come from God, that the omission is reverential, that God’s grace leads Him to expound truth rather than falsehood, or that the change of expression proves nothing. Al-Mizan regards this dispute as misplaced: deviation is a non-entity, not a created path, so it need not be attributed to either God or another creator. Where misguidance is attributed to God, it means His withholding of guidance, not His directing a person along another path.

Divine leading astray is consequently retribution, not an original decree of error. God has already supplied guidance through human fiṭra and prophetic instruction. A person begins misguidance by freely choosing evil, disobedience, and refusal to repent; if he persists, God confirms that state as punishment. Thus the initial loss of the path belongs to the person himself.
verses.10: Al-Mizan sees this as opening a new enumeration of divine blessings: water from heaven sustains human drink and the vegetation on which herds graze. Tusīmūn means grazing livestock, and shajar here extends from plants with stems and leaves to vegetation generally. The first min-hu marks distinction, while the second denotes the source.
verses.11: Al-Mizan explains that zaytūn, nakhīl, and aʿnāb can denote both the trees or vines and their fruits. “Fruits of all kinds” means that God causes to grow the trees of every fruit; olives, dates, and vines are singled out perhaps because they were especially common foods. This comprehensive provision for humans and animals is a sign of God’s unique providence for those who reflect.
verses.12: Al-Mizan explains that night and day, and each of the sun, moon, and stars, have distinct properties and effects that testify to God’s unique lordship. The verse therefore speaks of multiple “signs,” unlike neighboring verses using the singular, because of the plurality and diversity of these evidences.
verses.13:
Al-Mizan explains dharaʾa as “created,” and mukhtalifan alwānu-hu as the differing colors of earthly minerals and compounds from which people benefit; the variation of colors may also signify variation of kinds. The diversity of earthly plants, trees, fruits, and other created things is one sign of God’s unique lordship, hence the singular āya.

The three descriptions of those who recognize the signs correspond to three kinds of argument. The sign in vegetation and fruits rests on simple premises accessible through reflection. The signs in night, day, sun, moon, and stars rest on scientific premises understood by those knowledgeable of celestial movements and their effects. The sign in earthly diversity rests on general philosophical premises: those who take admonition grasp that a changing world requires a cause, that material things reduce to a common substance, and that their differences must return to something beyond matter.
verses.14:
Al-Mizan treats the sea as a further class of divine bounty. Tariyyan means moist and fresh; its fresh meat is fish, and its ornaments are pearls and corals. Mawākhir fī-hā describes ships cleaving the water to either side. “You see” is a general address to any observer, not a shift to addressing the Prophet.

Ships and sea travel enable people to seek God’s provision. The sea’s resources are an additional grace beyond the land’s sufficient necessities, bestowed so that people may become grateful. Ordinary necessities are often overlooked as blessings, whereas such supplementary bounties more readily make people conscious of God’s grace and of His power to withdraw even their necessities.
verses.15:
Al-Mizan explains an tamīda bi-kum as God’s placing firm mountains in the earth so that it does not rock people to and fro and disrupt their lives. He made streams to supply agriculture, orchards, and domestic animals, and made ways by which people find their destination. These ways include natural routes between lands and paths formed or constructed by people. Their attribution to God is no difficulty: even humanly made things are effects of His creation, created through the mediation of human action.

ʿAlāmāt are landmarks or signs by which people infer what lies beyond immediate perception; they include natural and conventional indicators, such as signs, words, gestures, and lines. People are also guided by stars. The third-person expression avoids repeating “you may be guided.”

The spiritual guidance of (16:9) is interjected amid physical blessings. Though it might seem more natural after the mention of star-guidance, its present placement prevents confusion between spiritual and physical guidance. The discourse now turns to the three foundations of divinity and lordship: God alone creates, bestows blessings, and knows what is inward and outward.

verses.17:
Al-Mizan presents this rhetorical question as the conclusion of the preceding proofs of God’s sole lordship. God creates all things, bestows the innumerable benefits on which cosmic order depends, and knows human beings inwardly and outwardly. He alone therefore owns, governs, sustains, and is worthy of worship. The idols have none of these attributes.

The argument is not merely an attempt to prove one Creator, for idolaters already acknowledged that God created everything, including their idols, and that idols themselves created nothing. Their error was to suppose that God had delegated providential rule and intercession to the idols. Since all benefits arise from God’s creations and remain under His untransferable ownership, God alone is the true benefactor; neither the benefits nor any supposed deity possesses an independent share in beneficence.

Creation and benefits alone are not the entire proof, for otherwise people might worship such means as rain-bearing clouds. The deity worthy of worship must also know worshipers’ outward acts and inward intentions, so that He can direct every creature toward its destined perfection and recognize sincere worship. Thus the verses form one argument for God’s exclusive lordship. “Is He who creates like one who does not create?” denies any equality between God and the false deities invoked beside Him: He creates, owns, and governs beings and all their effects, whereas they do not.
verses.18:
Al-Mizan explains that God’s blessings cannot be counted because, within the order of the cosmos, every existent is a blessing, even though a thing may not appear beneficial in every relation. Their universality follows from God’s all-forgivingness and mercy. Through maghfira, meaning concealment, He covers things’ defects and deficiencies; through raḥma, He completes what is lacking and removes needs. Whatever thereby becomes good or beneficial to another is a blessing for it. God’s blessings are consequently as universal as His forgiveness and mercy.

The verse thus invokes God’s forgiveness without reference to sin: here forgiveness concerns the covering of ontological deficiencies, not merely disobedience to divine commands.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan identifies knowledge as the third pillar of lordship. A deity must know the hidden and manifest states of servants; otherwise worship and disregard would be indistinguishable, and devotion would have no meaningful reality. Since genuine worship depends on inward sincerity as well as outward acts and words, the Lord worthy of worship must perceive both.

The wording “Allah knows whatever you hide and whatever you disclose” directly suits this context. Rather than simply asserting knowledge of all things, it emphasizes the concealed intentions and visible actions that determine the reality and value of worship. God’s complete knowledge, together with His creation and provision, establishes His exclusive worthiness to be worshiped.
verses.20: Al-Mizan explains that the idols and false gods lack the first pillar of lordship, creation. Since bestowing benefits is itself a creative act and derives from creation, they also lack the second pillar, beneficence. They are therefore neither gods nor lords; God alone is the true Lord.
verses.21:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse denies the third pillar of lordship to idols: knowledge of their devotees’ hidden and manifest states. Calling them “dead, not living” first affirms death and then emphatically denies life, thereby negating every kind of consciousness and knowledge. Their ignorance of when people will be resurrected is especially decisive because resurrection is the time of recompense, which a deity worthy of worship would have to know.

The first plural in “they … are not aware” refers to the idols, while the second, in “when they will be resurrected,” refers to the polytheists. It is wrong to take both pronouns as referring to the idols, since ignorance of the Day’s timing is not peculiar to idols but belongs to all besides God; it is still more mistaken to refer both to the polytheists.

Although the immediate argument concerns idols, it also refutes the divinity of the angels, jinn, holy men and women, celestial bodies, and whatever spirits idols are thought to represent. None creates, bestows benefits, or possesses knowledge inherently and independently; any such quality they possess comes through God alone. The shift to the third person perhaps indirectly addresses the polytheists when the Resurrection and Judgment, which they deny, are mentioned.

“Your God is One God” (16:22) follows necessarily: only God fulfills the conditions of divinity, while the alleged deities are neither creators, benefactors, nor intrinsically knowing. The sole being worthy of worship is therefore God.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse follows from the preceding proofs of complete monotheism. Such monotheism entails belief in the one all-knowing and omnipotent Creator, in the messages brought by His messengers, and in the return to Him for judgment, reward, and punishment. Thus disbelief in the Hereafter here identifies disbelief in God and His messengers as well, since belief in the Day of Reckoning implies both.

Their hearts are amiss (munkira) because they deny the truth, and they are arrogant (mustakbirūn) because they disdain it and refuse submission in order to appear powerful. Since the divine oneness is established by clear signs and admits no reasonable doubt, their denial is obstinate hostility toward truth, unsupported by evidence or argument.
verses.23: Al-Mizan explains that lā jarama is a composite expression of certainty and emphasis, ordinarily used in response to a preceding statement. The verse therefore affirms with certainty that God knows all that people conceal and disclose. This is an implicit warning: He knows their secret and open deeds, will call them to account and punish their disbelief and haughtiness, and does not love the arrogant.
verses.24:
Al-Mizan, following al-Mubarrad, takes asāṭīr al-awwalīn to mean writings containing legends and superstitions held sacred by their adherents; others regard asāṭīr as a plural of plurals derived from “line.” The questioner may have been a believer testing the disbelievers, an idolater asking mockingly, or a sincere inquirer; the context seems to favor one of the latter two. By calling the revelation “Myths of the ancients,” they declare it inherited human falsehood rather than revelation from God.

Awzār are heavy burdens, hence sins. Al-Mizan cites a Prophetic tradition, transmitted through both Shiʿi and Sunni chains and corroborated by the Qurʾan: one who establishes a good or bad practice receives a reward or burden like that of those who subsequently follow it, without diminishing what those followers receive. This does not violate “No bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another (35:18),” which concerns transferring a burden so that its original bearer is released. In outward interpretation, the originator or commander receives a burden equivalent to the doer’s, while the doer remains fully accountable. In reality, the evil act and its punishment are one, but because both the instigator and agent participate in it, that single punishment manifests for both; this accords with the personification of deeds.

The purposive lām in “that they may bear” connects their saying “Myths of the ancients” with their intent to mislead. They bear all their own burdens, while min in “some of the burdens” restricts what they bear from others to the sins resulting from their own misguidance—not a portion of all the followers’ sins, nor a division of each sin between them. The followers bear their own acts, and the leaders bear the consequences of inducing them. Accordingly, interpretations that make “entire” mean that disbelievers’ sins can never be expiated, or that contrast their punishment with mitigation specially granted believers, miss the verse’s sole concern: distinguishing the followers’ burdens from those incurred by the misleaders’ own act of misleading. Treating min as superfluous is still weaker.

“Without any knowledge (bi ghayr ʿilm)” means that the followers accepted the claim without proof. The speakers were leaders of misguidance and those deceived by them were imitators; both are condemned by “Look! Evil is what they bear!”

verses.26: Al-Mizan takes the razing of the edifice from its foundations and the collapse of its roof as a metaphor for God’s nullification of earlier peoples’ plots and exposure of their deceptions from a direction they did not expect. He removes the very foundation of their scheme while they attend to its apparent upper structure, so that it collapses upon them. The punishment that overtook them is worldly punishment. The verse consequently warns idolaters scheming against God and His Messenger that God turned the plots of earlier rebellious nations back upon them.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan explains yukhzī-him as a disgrace that brings shame. Tushāqqūn fī-him, derived from separation, denotes the polytheists’ hostile dissension from the people of monotheism over their alleged partners, although humanity was created upon the natural religion of monotheism. On the Day of Resurrection God will shame them through severe punishment and ask where those partners are for whose sake they divided themselves from the people of truth.

Those given knowledge are those to whom the reality of divine oneness has been unveiled. They will declare that disgrace and distress have come upon the faithless, whose supposed objects of worship will be exposed as empty names and mirages. Since only one permitted by the All-beneficent and speaking rightly speaks on that Day, the context indicates that these knowers are protected from falsehood in speech and deed: they see, do, and say only truth. Thus, in this verse they are the Infallibles. This is a contextual conclusion, not a claim that “those who were given knowledge” always denotes the Infallibles; other Qurʾanic occurrences concern non-infallible people. The verse supplies no evidence for restricting the phrase here to prophets, knowledgeable believers, believers generally, or angels.
verses.28:
Al-Mizan takes “Those whom the angels take away while they are wronging themselves” as an exposition of “the faithless” in the preceding verse, just as the later description of those taken while pure explains the Godwary. It is not thereby part of the speech of those given knowledge.

Fa alqaw al-salam means that the disbelievers offer surrender, humility, and obedience when the angels take their souls while they remain engrossed in wrongdoing and disbelief. At death they falsely protest that they did no evil, but their submission is rejected: God has always known what they used to do.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan explains that the address is collective, like the preceding addresses to the faithless. Each disbeliever enters through the gate of Hell suited to his own sins; the verse does not mean that every person enters through all its gates or through several of them.

Mutakabbirīn and mustakbirīn are close in meaning but differ in nuance. A mustakbir seeks self-aggrandizement and strives to display it, whereas a mutakabbir has made arrogance an established trait of character.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan holds that alladhīna ittaqū describes those continuously distinguished by Godwariness in worldly life. In contrast to the broader muttaqīn used later, this identifies the most complete in piety and faith, just as the preceding questioning concerned those complete in disbelief; it does not simply mean all believers who avoid idolatry or some sins.

Their answer, “Good,” means that God has sent down goodness: the Qurʾan, containing the knowledge and laws by which human happiness is attained in this world and the Hereafter. It therefore affirms both that the Qurʾan is divinely sent down and that it contains the keys to happiness, directly answering those who called it “myths of the ancients.”

The ensuing promise of good for those who do good explains their answer. Al-Mizan considers “and the abode of the Godwary is surely excellent” to be God’s direct speech, elaborating the worth of the Qurʾan, rather than the Godwary assigning themselves the Gardens of Eden. A good reward is a dignified recompense: obedience to the Qurʾan produces a righteous community governed by justice and benevolence and thus a good worldly life, while the Hereafter is better because its joy endures without affliction or disappointment. God finally praises the excellent abode of the Godwary before describing it further.
verses.31:
Al-Mizan explains that these verses describe the Godwary at death, in contrast to the arrogant who are taken while wronging themselves. Ṭayyib means free from what sullies or spoils a thing. Unlike ṭāhir, which denotes original purity free from what provokes revulsion, ṭayyib denotes an original state unspoiled by any contaminating element, whether or not it causes aversion; it is therefore often opposed to khabīth.

The Godwary are thus taken by the angels while free from the contamination of wrongdoing, including idolatry and other sins. The angels’ “Peace be to you!” assures them of safety, and “Enter paradise because of what you used to do” guides them to Paradise. Their state accords with: “Those who have faith and do not taint their faith with wrongdoing—for such there shall be safety, and they are the guided (6:82).” Interpretations limiting ṭayyib to freedom from idolatry, purity of speech and action, or purification from sins in general each have deficiencies.

verses.33:
Al-Mizan explains that the discourse returns to the arrogant idolaters and threatens them with either the angels’ descent to inflict ruinous punishment or the coming of their Lord’s edict, namely the Resurrection and its judgment and requital. Although “Allah’s edict is coming” elsewhere could possibly mean divine aid and Islam’s triumph over idolatry, that reading is weak here because of the passage’s severe tone and its subsequent treatment of denial of the Resurrection. The attribution “your Lord” to the Prophet also indicates a victory for him over his enemies.

Earlier peoples likewise denied the signs and mocked truth until punishment came upon them. God did not wrong them: He granted respite until their wrongdoing became persistent and established, and then punished them. Thus their punishment originated in their own continuous self-wronging, not divine injustice.
verses.34: Al-Mizan understands ḥāqa bihim as God's punishment enveloping them; another reading takes it as punishment descending on them—the punishment their prophets had warned them about and they derided. The rest is clear.
verses.35:
Al-Mizan explains that (16:35) expressly identifies the speakers as polytheists because their argument is directed against prophethood: “Had Allah wished, we and our fathers would not have worshipped anything besides Him or declared anything sacred without Him.” The object of “wished” is omitted because the consequence supplies it: had God willed their exclusive worship of Him, or their abandonment of other worship, they would have complied.

The objection that divine will cannot attach to a non-action is metaphysically beside the linguistic point. Ordinary and figurative speech can attribute the occurrence of non-existence to will, and the prophets’ prohibitions themselves demand cessation. If one nevertheless insists that will must attach to something positive, the statement can mean that, had God decreed their ceasing to worship others, their idolatry would not have occurred. The two uses of min emphasize that they would have worshipped nothing whatever apart from Him. “Neither we nor our fathers” reflects their inherited imitation, while the parallel claim about making things sacred concerns such unauthorized prohibitions as the baḥīrah and sāʾibah.

The polytheists acknowledged God alone as Creator but denied His exclusive right to worship: among their many supposed gods, the Creator was not worshipped, while the objects they worshipped were not regarded as creators. Their argument invokes God’s unfailing creative will, not His legislative will. They reason that, if the prophets’ prohibitions truly came from God, an irresistible divine will would have prevented their idolatry and their declaring lawful things forbidden; the continued existence of those practices supposedly proves that no divine command, prohibition, message, or law exists concerning them.

Al-Mizan carefully rejects readings that make them say God positively willed and compelled their idolatry. The counterfactual law indicates that, in their claim, God did not will its abandonment; it does not assert that He affirmatively decreed the act. Nor were they admitting themselves misguided through predestination: elsewhere they claim that they and their fathers are guided (43:20–22), so an interpretation that makes their plea acknowledge wretchedness contradicts their position. They also were not asserting delegation (tafwīḍ), as though their acts were independent of divine will and God could stop them only by placing external obstacles in their way; had that been their point, they would have said that God could have prevented them. The verse’s evident conditional does not say this.

Their intended claim is therefore narrower: because God’s creative will did not irresistibly attach to abandoning idolatry, the prophetic legislative prohibition must be false. The Qur’an answers by distinguishing the two wills. God’s guidance through revelation is legislative and respects human choice; a messenger’s sole responsibility is clear communication, completion of the proof, warning, and glad tidings—not compelling belief by the creative command that admits no resistance. The same excuse was made by earlier polytheists and did not invalidate their messengers. The Prophet should therefore continue conveying the decisive message and disregard these fabricated justifications. The conclusion, “Is the messengers’ duty anything but to communicate in clear terms?”, exposes the fallacy: human messengers convey revealed laws ordered to worldly and otherworldly welfare, while their hearers remain responsible for choosing faith or rejection, as also indicated by (6:50) and (18:110).
verses.36:
Al-Mizan explains ṭāghūt as what transgresses rightful limits, including every transgressor and every being worshiped besides God; the term may be singular or plural. God’s raising of a messenger in every nation is a universal divine practice suited to all peoples’ needs. The essence of every mission is the invitation to worship God and avoid Ṭāghūt. Such an invitation is not coercion: a messenger’s command and prohibition call people to act, and do not force their compliance.

Every nation consequently divides into those whom God guides to His worship and avoidance of false gods, and those for whom error has become established. Guidance belongs solely to God, yet this does not entail predestination: people make the initial movement toward guidance through preserving their innate disposition, striving in good deeds, and, after a lapse, repentance. Divine guidance then comes as reward. The initially misguided choose error through wrongdoing, desire, disbelief, and similar acts; God’s subsequent withholding or confirmation of guidance is punitive, not an original creation of their error.

The verse’s wording avoids simply saying that God led the second group astray, lest He be thought the originator of misguidance. Misguidance is not a positive thing created alongside guidance, but the absence and loss of the perfection of guidance. When a person progressively ruins the capacity for guidance and persists without repentance, God leaves him in his chosen error and confirms it as retribution.

The command to travel the earth addresses the idolaters who objected that a prophetic call would have compelled them. Ruined nations demonstrate instead that messengers issue a humanly intelligible call of warning and glad tidings to worship God and shun false gods, and that deniers meet divine retribution. Prophethood does not consist in forcing obedience.
verses.37:
Al-Mizan explains that those whose error has been confirmed are beyond the reach of the Prophet’s eagerness. Since God alone guides, had guidance remained possible for them He would have guided them; instead, on account of their own evil choices and deeds, He has confirmed their misguidance. God does not reverse His decree, and no helper can overcome Him. The verse therefore consoles the Messenger and does not attribute an initial injustice to God.

The commentary reports that Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī understood the polytheists’ statement as an objection that divine determination would make prophethood futile, and held that their fault was using it to excuse idolatry and challenge God’s judgments. Al-Zamakhsharī treated it as deterministic reasoning, maintaining that God does not will polytheism or sin and that servants perform such acts freely. Al-Mizan judges that this determinism–free-will dispute misses the immediate point: the polytheists were using their conduct to deny that the prophets’ prohibition was truly divine, arguing that God would otherwise have made them refrain. That argument is false regardless of the broader theological dispute.

“They will have no helpers” means that, although help exists for others on the Day of Judgment, these polytheists will have none at all. The helpers available to the guided are noble angels and other means of divine success and guidance, together with God’s grace and intercession.
verses.38:
Al-Mizan explains that jahd aymānihim means that they exerted themselves to make their oaths as forceful as possible. Their oath that God will not resurrect the dead rejects both resurrection and the Day of Judgment, treating death as final extinction. This does not conflict with a belief in reincarnation, which posits a soul’s transition into another living form in this world rather than resurrection after death.

The divine answer declares resurrection a binding, irrevocable promise God has undertaken to fulfill. Most people do not know this because they disregard the signs that establish it: the creation of the heavens and earth, the diversity of human conduct between wrongdoing and righteousness, and the commands of divine law.
verses.39:
Al-Mizan explains that li- is purposive: God resurrects the dead in order to make clear what people differed about, so that the faithless will know they lied in denying resurrection. These are ultimately one purpose, because the resolution of their disputes with the prophets necessarily reveals their lie, and all disputes about the Day of Judgment are resolved when its reality is witnessed.

The relevant disagreement concerns true religion—belief and practice—as conveyed in the Books and by the prophets, not differences of bodily features. Resolving such disputes is a principal feature of the Day of Judgment, of which the bridge (ṣirāṭ), records of deeds, weighing, reckoning, and judgment are extensions. The clarification then is not merely worldly instruction through scripture, preaching, wisdom, or argument, but manifest reality: the veil is removed, no doubt remains, and people directly recognize the truth of contested religious teachings, the worth of righteous deeds, and the futility of persistent evil.
verses.40:
Al-Mizan explains that comparison with the parallel verse in Sūrah Yā Sīn identifies God’s command (amr) with His saying or word (qawl). The Qurʾan also calls this decisive, irresistible reality His decree, judgment, and word (kalima). God’s creation—the bestowal of existence—is thus encompassed by His command, utterance, and word; His word is manifested in His decisive saying, “Be!”

God first wills and decrees a thing, and then brings it into existence by His command. His word is true both as speech and as the external reality it produces; consequently His acts contain no falsehood, error, or failure, His command cannot be resisted, and His promise is invariably fulfilled.

The verse, read with the preceding discussion of the polytheists, distinguishes two divine wills. The creative will (irādat al-takwīni) is absolute and unchangeable, whereas the legislative will (irādat al-tashrīʿ) is addressed to human beings and may be obeyed or defied.
verses.41:
Al-Mizan treats this as a promise to those who migrate solely for God’s pleasure after being wronged for His cause. Although believers migrated both to Abyssinia and, with the Prophet, from Mecca to Medina, the context more readily fits the migration to Medina.

“Settling them in this world in a good place” may mean granting them a good land in exchange for what they left, or a good condition such as victory and triumph. Both readings converge: their migration sought the establishment of a just, righteous Islamic community devoted to God, not material advantages of land or climate. The worldly good is the realization of that community. The Hereafter’s reward is still greater: happiness without hardship, everlasting life, pleasure without pain, and nearness to the Lord of the Worlds.
verses.42:
Al-Mizan explains that the promise concerns whoever migrates for God, whether or not the person had already migrated when the verse was revealed. “Those who endured and upon their Lord they rely” therefore principally describes the emigrants by the patience and reliance on God required to attain the promised worldly and otherworldly outcome. Without endurance in striving, resistance to despair, and reliance on God rather than their own limited power, their community would have collapsed and its rewards been lost.

If the verse instead addresses those who had already migrated, the phrase is praise for their sacrifice of homes and wealth, their endurance of Meccan hostility for God’s sake, and their steadfast trust in Him throughout adherence to Islam.
verses.43:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse answers the polytheists’ claim that, had Allah willed, they would not have worshipped other than Him. Messengers are ordinary human men who receive revelation and summon people to what benefits them in this world and the Hereafter; their call does not overturn the natural order or abolish human free choice. The verse is thus not principally a reply to an alleged demand that angels, rather than humans, should be messengers, for that claim is absent from the context.

Nor is its purpose to specify the age at which messengers begin their missions. Although “sent” can include prophets as well as messengers, and some have inferred that neither office belongs to children or women, Jesus’ declaration of prophethood in infancy and John’s receiving judgment while a boy prevent this from being the verse’s point. Its point is that messengers such as Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and John were mortal men granted revelation, not possessors of unseen creative powers.

“So ask the people of the remembrance if you do not know” apparently addresses the Prophet and his people in a generalized sense: those who do not know should ask those who know, while the Prophet and believers do not need such inquiry. Although it may be read as directed to the polytheists, this would require an unsupported shift from a singular to a plural addressee. Dhikr is what preserves or recalls meaning and, in Qur’anic usage without a qualifying context, commonly concerns remembrance of God. The Qur’an and previous revealed scriptures are therefore “reminders,” and those versed in and committed to them are their people.

Since the polytheists rejected the Prophet and mocked the Qur’an, the people of the reminder here apparently means, in particular, the followers of the Torah, whom the polytheists regarded more favorably than believers. Reading the phrase as experts in past history regardless of faith is an unsupported metaphorical extension, while limiting it to the Prophet, believers, and followers of the Qur’an does not serve the argument, since the audience did not accept them. The verse nevertheless conveys the rational principle that the ignorant refer to experts; it is not itself a legislated religious command to ask scholars.

“With manifest proofs and scriptures” means that the former messengers were sent with decisive evidence validating their prophethood and scriptures preserving their teachings. The reminder sent down to the Prophet and that sent down to people are one revelation, received through him so that people may adopt and practice it. His task is to receive, convey, and clarify the gradually revealed divine knowledge, which people cannot independently obtain.

The commentary holds that the intended reflection is especially upon the Prophet himself, rather than merely upon the reminder. His orphanhood, obscurity, lack of formal learning and righteous guardian, poverty, and life among an unenlightened people show that the profound scripture he brought could not have been acquired or produced by him; it came solely from God’s knowledge and power. The alternative reading—that the reminder was sent so that he might explain its contents and people might reflect upon it as revelation—creates an apparent redundancy, since the same revelation would be sent to him to explain what had already been sent to them.

verses.45:
Al-Mizan describes this and the following verses as a warning to polytheists who worshipped others, made their own laws and rites, abandoned prophetic ordinances, and opposed God and His messengers through false arguments and arrogance. “Those who plotted evil deeds” means those who deceitfully committed evil deeds, not merely those who devised “evil plots”; the latter grammatical interpretation does not fit the context.

After signs have established God’s unmatched lordship and shown prophethood to be a divinely guided call to human good in this world and the Hereafter, such people cannot reasonably feel secure. The verse threatens them, including the Meccans, with God’s punishment: the earth may swallow them, or punishment may reach them unexpectedly.
verses.46:
Al-Mizan takes the One who may seize them to be God, as the Qur’an commonly attributes akhdh to Him, though some interpret the subject as punishment. Taqallub, “movements,” denotes the polytheists’ changing states, evil intentions and deeds, and their pursuit of transient worldly enjoyments.

Their seizure amid these movements means that God—or, on the alternative reading, punishment—overtakes them while they engage in sin and plot against God and His messenger. It is possible that their very blessings become the means of punishment. “They could not escape” explains that they can neither overcome God nor evade His will.
verses.47:
Al-Mizan explains takhawwuf as fear instilled in the heart. Seizure “with fear” is punishment preceded by apprehensive signs, allowing those affected an opportunity to avert its full arrival through repentance and remorse; it contrasts with punishment that comes suddenly without warning.

Some interpret it as frightening but nonfatal events such as earthquakes or storms. Others understand takhawwuf as gradual diminution: God successively removes security, rain, prosperity, abundance, health, and other blessings.
verses.48:
Al-Mizan says that “see” directs sensory attention to the things casting shadows. Yatafayyuʾ zilalu-hu refers to the movement of their shadows, especially in the afternoon; zill is broader than fayʾ. “Right and left” encompasses the distinct shadows cast on all such sides, and dakhirīn denotes submission and humility.

The daily shifting of shadows shows that all created things are continually prostrating and submitting to God. The verse challenges polytheists who reject monotheism and prophethood: even shadows display natural obeisance, as do all terrestrial and celestial beings, including angels, jinn, and revered humans whom they wrongly worship. This universal submission manifests one sovereign whose exclusive right is worship and humble obedience. Monotheism is recognizing God alone as deserving submission, and religion is adherence to His commands.
verses.49:
Al-Mizan distinguishes the preceding symbolic prostration of shadows from the real prostration here of every creature in the heavens and earth. Prostration is genuine humility and complete submission to divine majesty; bodily prostration counts as worship only insofar as it expresses that reality. Humans and jinn belong among moving creatures, whereas angels are mentioned separately, indicating that their descending, ascending, and traversing are unlike the physical spatial movement of earthly creatures. The verse also indicates living beings in the celestial realms. All beings thus surrender to God’s command, so worship and prostration belong exclusively to Him.

Istikbār is blameworthy self-exaltation: toward creatures, it is unjust superiority among equally dependent beings; toward God, it falsely claims independence and leads to disregarding His commands. Kibriyāʾ, God’s inherent majesty, is fitting for Him, whereas mustakbir implies an aspiring and baseless claim to greatness. The angels’ lack of arrogance means both that their nature is constantly mindful of God and that their conduct never rebels.

“They fear their Lord above them” describes not fear of punishment but an intrinsic awe before God’s supreme power and majesty. “Above them” indicates that this reverence arises from His dominance over them. “They do what they are commanded” negates practical arrogance as well: angels do not disobey, forget, become distracted, or neglect God’s will.

Their particular mention refutes idolaters who deified angels and similar beings, while showing that angels are among creation’s most devoted servants. The commentary rejects the inference that angels have legal duties like humans or that their fear necessarily entails hope: Qur’anic imperatives do not always imply obligation, and this fear is reverence rather than fear of retribution. Nor does the verse establish angels’ superiority over faithful, virtuous humans; it only sets them above sinful unbelievers in this context of praise.

verses.51:
Al-Mizan connects this command most fittingly with the preceding universal prostration to God. Rahba, “fear,” is opposed to raghba, affectionate inclination or desire.

“Do not take two gods” forbids every form of taking a god besides God, not merely two gods. “Indeed, He is one God” establishes that worship must be exclusive to Him. The number two may particularly answer a polytheistic division between a creator god and a separate god of governance and worship: creation and governance are inseparable, so the one Creator is also the sole Manager and sole object of worship.

The fronting in “so fear only Me (fa-iyyāya farhabūn)” stresses exclusivity. It calls idolaters away from worshipping angels, jinn, and humans whom they thought governed worldly affairs and could secure blessings. In this setting, fearing God alone is an expression for worshipping and revering Him alone, with the awe due to His majesty rather than merely fear of punishment.
verses.52:
Al-Mizan holds that this verse, with the next, proves God’s exclusive divinity and right to worship: religion belongs to Him alone, and no other being may legislate religious law or be obeyed as such. Al-Rāghib reports that wāṣib can mean enduring or obligatory, while its association with lasting punishment has led some to read the verse as a threat of perpetual punishment to those who take two gods. In context, dīn most fittingly means the divinely established order by which people obey God permanently.

Everything in the heavens and earth belongs to God in the fullest sense: it exists through Him in an unbroken relation like a possession inseparable from its owner. As the true Owner and Manager, He cannot have an independent governor operating apart from Him. His lordship therefore requires reverence and submission.

Since God alone owns and governs the universe and knows what leads humanity to prosperity, He alone has authority to establish the religious order and its laws. Interpretations of dīn as obedience, sovereignty, or recompense have been proposed, but this meaning best suits the context of exclusive lordship and prophetic religion. “Do you then fear other than God?” rhetorically denies that anyone besides Him should be revered or obeyed.
verses.53:
Al-Mizan presents the verse as further proof of God’s unity in lordship against polytheistic beliefs and self-made laws. Every blessing comes from God. Harm is the loss of a benefit necessary to human well-being, and tajʾarūn evokes the distressed cry of wild animals; turning to Him in such distress is a figurative description of supplication and seeking help.

People’s exclusive cry to God when harm touches them shows that they recognize Him as the source of blessings and the remover of hardship. Were there another true refuge, they would turn to it, yet in extremity they do not. Their instinctive appeal therefore exposes the inconsistency of withholding exclusive worship and obedience from Him.

When ordinary means fail and all visible supports disappear, the heart’s continuing hope necessarily has an object beyond those broken means. This enduring cause, unaffected by crises and never absent from humanity, is God. The truth is rooted in human nature but can be veiled by external influences and worldly attractions; overwhelming crisis strips these away and makes the heart turn instinctively to God, the Cause of causes.
verses.54:
Al-Mizan begins here the reproach of polytheists that leads to a threat of punishment. Once God removes their distress after their instinctive appeal to their Creator, they should recognize Him as the sole Lord. Instead, some return to idolatry, fastening on external causes as partners; their vices and desires again blind them.

The lām in li-yakfurū, “being unthankful,” indicates purpose: their association of partners serves to deny God’s blessings and to refuse gratitude for relief. Immersion in material causes makes them remember only immediate sources of benefit, rather than God, the Causer of causes. They become dependent and fearful regarding those sources, while showing God neither humility nor concern. Thus their persistent polytheism is persistent ingratitude and rejection of God’s favors.

The shift from speaking about them to addressing them directly—“So let them enjoy. Soon they shall know!”—is a threat. The unspecified enjoyment includes every worldly indulgence, for which they will be called to account, and the unspecified future knowledge leaves their punishment unforeseen and thereby intensifies the warning. The interpretation of the lām as a lām of command is considered needlessly strained.

Al-Mizan explains that the verse adds another sin of the polytheists: they allot part of God’s provision to mā lā yaʿlamūn, their alleged gods, though these possess neither harm nor benefit. This may refer directly to offerings assigned to idols, such as shares of crops and livestock.

It may also continue the preceding statement about associating partners: they dedicate a share of their provision to apparent causes whose real nature and efficacy they do not know. Although they treat such causes as partners in provision, their pleas to God in distress reveal an underlying recognition that God is the true provider. Their attribution therefore makes visible causes co-contributors alongside Him, and they are solemnly warned that they will be questioned about these fabrications.
verses.57:
Al-Mizan reproaches the polytheists for assigning daughters to God while reserving for themselves what they desired, namely sons. They called female deities God’s daughters; some commentators report that Khuzāʿah and Kinānah held angels to be His daughters. Similar beliefs concerning female angels and jinn occurred in Brahmanical, Buddhist, and Sabian idolatry, and the Qur’an mentions both their calling the angels female and their assigning a lineage between God and jinn.

Explanations that angels were called female because they are unseen, or because their hiddenness resembles the seclusion of daughters, are speculative. The commentary traces this notion more broadly to ancient polytheistic traditions of India, Egypt, Babylon, Greece, and Rome. Idolaters treated angels as sources of good and jinn as sources of evil, then imagined active and passive cosmic forces as father and mother, with their products divided into sons and daughters. Arab claims that angels were God’s daughters were thus blind imitation of older polytheistic beliefs.

The apparent meaning is that they assigned daughters to God and sons to themselves, preferring for Him what they disliked. Some object on grammatical grounds that the second phrase cannot be connected directly to the act of assigning, but Al-Mizan maintains that such a rule applies only where confusion would result; the intervening preposition separates the pronouns. The direct connection is therefore sound.
verses.58: Al-Mizan explains that a darkened face denotes anger, while kaẓīm is one who suppresses sorrow and rage. The clause is adverbial: at the very time polytheists assigned daughters to God, a man receiving news that his wife had borne a daughter would darken with anger and restrain it within himself.
verses.59:
Al-Mizan explains yatawārā as hiding or turning away, huwan as humiliation, and dass as concealing. On receiving news of a daughter’s birth, the idolater hid from people in distress, considering whether to keep her in perceived disgrace or bury her alive. The passage describes this entrenched practice of infanticide, associated with fear of poverty and fear that daughters might be taken by those deemed unworthy.

A reported account traces its beginning to Banī Tamīm after Persian forces captured their women; when some chose to remain after a truce, the men resolved to bury future daughters, and other tribes adopted the practice. “Evil is the judgment that they make” most fittingly condemns their judgment that daughters belong to God while sons belong to themselves: they assigned to God what they considered undesirable and retained what they preferred. Some instead take it as condemning the supposed duty to kill daughters, but the first interpretation better fits the following verse.
verses.60:
Al-Mizan explains mathal as a description, so mathal al-sūʾ is the evil description belonging to those who deny the Hereafter. Descriptions include positive and negative qualities, whether innate or acquired; praise and blame properly concern voluntary qualities. True religion requires the distinction of good and evil, but moral disapproval alone does not restrain wrongdoing, since social customs can change. Firm belief in the Hereafter, reckoning, and punishment is what deters evil, gives conduct its proper meaning, and grounds virtuous action—indeed, it has a practical influence unmatched even by monotheism, though monotheism is the highest knowledge.

Disbelief in the Hereafter and neglect of accountability are therefore the root of sinful action and every evil description, while belief in it is the source of moral excellence. If believers commit evil, it results from a temporary forgetfulness of the Day of Judgment. The evil associated with unbelievers includes moral faults, naturally disliked conditions such as sickness, death, incapacity, and ignorance, and the deficiencies of need, poverty, non-being, and potentiality; some are peculiar to them, while others are shared by believers or universal to contingent beings.

God is transcendent above every evil description. He does not commit injustice, and every judgment and act of His follows wisdom and the order He established. He is also free from all weakness, ignorance, death, non-existence, need, and limitation. Even created beings’ positive attributes—life, knowledge, power, nobility, greatness, and majesty—are limited and dependent, whereas in God they are absolute and flawless.

“For God is the highest description” thus means that He alone possesses the supreme degree of every positive perfection, without any negative quality, defect, or likeness to creation. “He is the Almighty, the Wise” confirms that no disgrace or ignorance can attach to Him. The disbeliever, by contrast, is marked by disgrace and ignorance; the believer, despite inherent deficiency, is protected by God’s honor and brought from ignorance through His spirit.
verses.61:
Al-Mizan explains that “upon it” means upon the earth. Dābba may plausibly mean human beings in this context: if God punished every wrongdoer for wrongdoing, no human would remain, because the destruction of sinful forebears would also prevent the later birth of the virtuous, including prophets and impeccable saints. If dābba is taken broadly to include animals, their destruction follows the extinction of humanity, since other earthly creatures’ existence is bound to human survival and welfare.

The verse does not prove that prophets are fallible or personally guilty of wrongdoing. It says that comprehensive punishment of mankind would leave none, not that every individual would be punished for an individual sin; righteous persons could perish in the consequences of a community’s destruction. The explanations that “mankind” means only oppressors, that wrongdoing includes merely less-preferred acts applicable to prophets, or that punishment such as withheld rain affects righteous and wicked alike all have limitations. The first does not explain the destruction of the infallibles or other creatures; the second does not fit the context of polytheism and threatened punishment; and the third lacks textual support.

God does not hasten their reckoning but grants respite until an appointed term. For an individual, that term is death; for a community, extinction; and for humanity, the trumpet announcing Resurrection. When it arrives, it cannot be postponed or advanced even by an hour.
verses.62:
Al-Mizan returns to the polytheists’ attribution of daughters to God while they preferred sons for themselves. “They attribute to Allah what they dislike” specifically concerns daughters, and “their tongues assert the lie that the best reward will be theirs” is their false claim to a favorable outcome through keeping what they desired. Some understand “the best reward” as Paradise, should Resurrection and prophetic speech prove true, but the ensuing threat qualifies that reading.

Their fabrication assumes that they can assign God what they dislike while securing for themselves what they want, as though they could outstrip God. “Undoubtedly, the Fire shall be their lot” refutes this assumption: they are destined for the Fire. Mufraṭūn denotes those sent or advancing ahead, and hence their being foremost into it.
verses.63:
Al-Mizan takes “today” most appropriately as the day of revelation. God sent messengers to earlier nations, but Satan made their deeds attractive, so they followed him and turned from the messengers. Satan is consequently their ally at that time through their collective adherence to misguidance, while their painful punishment is the punishment of the Day of Judgment.

Al-Zamakhsharī’s view that Satan beautified the deeds of former nations but is now the ally of Quraysh is weakened by the change of pronouns. It is also possible that the nations are extinct peoples and that Satan’s guardianship of them is in Barzakh, where they suffer punishment. Other interpretations make “today” the whole worldly life, the Day of Judgment, or the past day when Satan adorned their deeds. The first reading is preferred, then the Barzakh reading, then the reading of worldly life.
verses.64: Al-Mizan explains that “for them” refers to the polytheists and their disagreements about true belief, knowledge, and righteous deeds. The Book was sent to the Prophet so that he might clarify these disputes and thereby complete God’s argument against them. Believers are mentioned separately: for those who have faith, the Book is guidance and mercy, guiding them to the truth and enveloping them in mercy as they accept and follow it.
verses.65: Al-Mizan explains that the verse draws attention to the earth’s renewal after winter dormancy: spring rain causes dormant roots and seeds to grow, and this vegetative growth is a real, though weaker, form of life than animal life. “Listening” means receptively accepting words that merit acceptance, as a truth-seeker attends to and retains what may be true. Thus, for those receptive to truth, God’s revival of the dead earth is evidence for resurrection: He who restores life to earth can revive the dead.
verses.66: Al-Mizan explains that “waste” is the intestinal matter called dung when expelled, while sāʾighan denotes a drink that is pleasant and passes easily down the throat. Cattle—camels, cows, and sheep—offer an admonishing sign to those willing to learn: milk is brought forth from among bodily waste and blood, which are internally near it, yet is distinguished from both and remains pure, without their taste or smell. This pure and pleasant milk manifests the breadth of God’s power and will; the One who preserves its purity amid such impurities can also revive human beings even after their bones decay and their parts disperse in the soil.
verses.67:
Al-Mizan takes sukr in its original sense to be the loss of sound awareness caused by an intoxicating substance; its other reported senses—an intoxicating drink, tasty food, calmness, and the verbal noun for becoming intoxicated or confused—are extensions of that primary meaning. The phrase concerning dates and grapes admits several grammatical analyses, but in each case its practical meaning is that people derive from them intoxicants, such as wine, and wholesome provisions, such as raisins and grape syrup.

The commentary insists that the verse neither declares intoxicants lawful nor commends making them. The contrast between sukr and “goodly provision” may itself be reproachful, showing that intoxicants are not good provision; even if this is not accepted, the verse’s purpose is not legislation but enumerating the uses then taken from these fruits as divine blessings that lead to monotheism. It therefore contains no ruling to be abrogated or preserved, and rejects the report attributed to Qatādah that a verse in Sūrah al-Māʾidah abrogated it.

Al-Mizan rejects the account reported by the author of Rūḥ al-Maʿānī—that wine was lawful in Mecca and later prohibited in Medina—maintaining that wine had already been prohibited before the Emigration, while the Medinan verse emphasized that prohibition and reproved those departing from it. It also rejects the view attributed to Ibn Abbas that sukr is Ethiopian for vinegar, since using a word that means wine in Arabic for vinegar would create implausible ambiguity, and sets aside the view attributed to Abū ʿUbaydah that it means a sweet snack.

The commentary likewise rejects the Ḥanafī claim that the verse permits a non-intoxicating amount of alcohol because sukr is a divine favor. The verse counts dates and grapes as blessings, not every lawful or unlawful human use of them; moreover, the contrast with “good sustenance” suggests admonition. Nothing in the wording limits sukr to raisins, drink, or a small quantity; if it established permissibility as a blessing, it would establish all intoxicants as permissible. Nor could something first be counted as a divine favor and later be called Satanic defilement. The closing phrase calls people to reason about plants and fruits.
verses.68:
Al-Mizan explains waḥī as a swift, subtle communication of a meaning concealed from others. Qur’anic usage includes instinctive inspiration in animals, dreams, whispering, and gestures, as well as God’s speech to prophets and messengers; yet Islamic religious usage properly reserves “revelation” for the latter. Here God inspired the honeybee through an instinct placed in its nature. Dhulul, plural of dhulūl, means tame or manifestly submissive.

The bee was inspired to make its dwelling in mountains, trees, and, apparently, places where hives are erected. Its being commanded to eat every fruit refers to nourishment derived from the materials of blossoms, from which fruits develop. The consequent command to follow meekly the ways of its Lord reinforces that this “eating” includes gathering and taking home what becomes stored honey, and that all its movements proceed through divine inspiration. Honey, issuing from its belly in diverse colours, is a cure for people in many diseases and is the result of the bee’s compliance with this divinely inspired order.

The verse is therefore a sign for those who reflect, since the bee’s remarkable social order and intricate life disclose their secrets through deep contemplation. Al-Mizan contrasts this ending with the nearby calls to “listen” concerning life and death, which naturally admonish, and to “apply reason” concerning fruits, whose useful interconnected order is rationally apprehended. It adds that the address to the Prophet may reflect the exceptional character of the bee’s system, and notes the chapter’s recurring shifts between addressing polytheists compassionately and turning to the Prophet when faced with their disbelief and obstinacy.
