verses.70: Al-Mizan explains ardhal al-ʿumur as the age of senility, when cognitive and perceptual powers decline so far that a person comes to know nothing after having known much; this varies by temperament and generally begins around seventy-five. God creates people and takes most at an ordinary age, while allowing some to reach this condition. The loss of knowledge and strength proves that life, death, consciousness, and knowledge are not in human control; otherwise people would preserve both their intellect and lives. Their ordered existence is instead bound to God’s knowledge and power, hence the conclusion, “Indeed Allah is all-knowing, all-powerful.”
verses.71:
Al-Mizan distinguishes quantitative differences in rizq, such as wealth and poverty, from the qualitative superiority intended here: freedom and independent authority to manage one’s possessions, as opposed to a slave’s dependence on the master’s permission. The verse concerns this latter superiority. Those granted it neither give, nor can give, their slaves an equal ownership and independence that would dissolve their own mastery. This untransferable superiority is a blessing bestowed by God; the verse reproaches those who deny that blessing.

The commentary holds that mastership and slavery, though socially constituted, have roots in human nature. It argues that even societies that formally abolish slavery retain its essence through the subjugation of whole societies, because rivalry for dominance persists. Such dominance benefits society, in its view, because the stronger group administers the affairs of the subordinate group.

The phrase “so that they become equal in its respect” derives from what is negated: the superior do not hand over their provision so that their slaves become equal partners, since that would end their mastery. It may also be read as an unexpressed, negative rhetorical question: since the superior do not grant this priority, are the two groups equal? They are not. The “blessing of Allah” is this superiority accompanied by freedom and independence.

Al-Mizan rejects the interpretation that the verse reproaches people for refusing to share wealth and wives with slaves and therefore refutes assigning partners to God. It also rejects linking it to the parable in Sūrah al-Rūm or to the Christians of Najran: this Meccan verse counts blessings to argue for monotheism, whereas the other verse reproaches polytheism, and the Prophet did not meet the Najran Christians until Medina. It further rejects the view that masters and slaves are equal before God in provision, because this negates the verse’s stated superiority and its reference to God’s blessing. Finally, it finds inadequate the reading that masters simply retain control of their property, since that is true with regard to anyone; mentioning slaves is meaningful only if the intended blessing is masters’ superiority and control over them.
verses.72:
Al-Mizan explains ḥafada as helpers and servants among one’s children, derived from a root denoting swift activity and service. It can consequently be understood as adult children in contrast to younger children, or as grandchildren; in either case, God grants offspring from spouses who assist people in their needs and help avert hardships. He also provides good things, including water, fruits whose production people did not cause, and provisions such as food and clothing acquired through their own efforts.

The verse then rebukes the polytheists for believing falsehood—idols, their attribution of daughters to God while claiming sons for themselves, and legislation of misguided leaders—while denying God’s blessing. Spouses of one’s own kind and the children and helpers arising from them are among the clearest and greatest blessings, forming the basis of human society, cooperation, and worldly and spiritual flourishing. If this natural bond were broken, no substitute could replace it; human unity would dissolve and humanity would perish. The verse thus introduces the condemnation of worshipping beings that control no provision from heaven or earth.
verses.73:
Al-Mizan considers the most suitable explanation to be that rizq refers to the recipient of provision and shayʾan is an apposition: the polytheists worship beings that have no power to provide them with anything. The wording may also indicate that these beings neither provide sustenance nor own anything whatever in the heavens and earth; “nor are they capable” emphasizes their utter incapacity to possess provision or anything else.

The verse treats idols in two respects. Since they are ordinarily stones, wood, gold, or silver, it uses the non-sentient mā; yet because their worshippers regard them as gods, it uses the masculine plural in wa lā yastaṭīʿūn. By returning from the enumeration of blessings to the idols’ helplessness, the verse begins to state the larger conclusion: monotheism, the denial of likenesses made for God, His unique lordship, the indication of prophethood and legislation through a parable, and resurrection.
verses.74: Al-Mizan understands “do not draw comparisons for Allah” as forbidding descriptions that liken God to created beings: for example, alleging that He has daughters, that angels are His daughters, that He has kinship with jinn, or questioning His power to revive decayed bones. Such “comparisons” are similitudes, not merely rival deities. People must not describe God by analogy with creation, for God knows whereas they do not know the realities or essence of God. The alternative interpretation, that the phrase simply prohibits setting up equivalents or rivals to God, is judged remote from the verse’s apparent meaning.
verses.75:
Al-Mizan explains the parable as contrasting the general kinds of a wholly owned, powerless slave and a free person whom God has given abundant provision and who spends from it openly and secretly. They plainly are not equal. The plural yastawūn, rather than the dual, shows that the comparison concerns these two classes rather than two particular individuals. It proves that God, the Provider and Owner of all things, cannot be equated with created beings that own and manage nothing, whether for themselves or others. The supposed partners of the polytheists are themselves owned and powerless.

“All praise belongs to Allah” concludes this proof. Ḥamd is recognition of a voluntary beautiful act, and all beautiful blessings and every praiseworthy attribute—creation, provision, mercy, forgiveness, kindness, and beneficence—belong uniquely to God. The phrase does not primarily mean gratitude, merely the force of the argument, or an instruction for servants to praise God for guidance; those interpretations are rejected.

“Most of them do not know” means that most polytheists do not recognize that all blessings, ownership, and power belong to God alone. They instead attribute a delegated share to their deities and worship them in hope of benefit or fear of harm. A smaller, elite group knows the truth but turns from it through arrogance and obstinacy. The commentary rejects the view that the parable contrasts disbelievers, whose deeds are nullified, with believers, whose deeds God accepts, because that does not fit the surrounding argument from God’s blessings for monotheism. The parable concerns God and the alleged associates in His lordship, establishing that the true Lord alone is the benefactor.
verses.76:
Al-Mizan explains abkam as one born mute, unable to understand or be understood through speech; kall as a burdensome dependent; and tawjīh as directing someone toward a task. The parable contrasts two opposite kinds of men. The first, deprived of hearing and speech, lacks the broad knowledge and communication that hearing supplies, has no effective power, depends upon his master, and produces no good wherever he is sent. The second is described summarily as one who enjoins justice and follows a straight path.

Justice is the middle course in action, free from excess and deficiency, not only fairness in rule. One who truly commands it must embody uprightness in character and conduct, and his call to others rests on his own adherence to the straight path rather than on unsupported preaching. The straight path is the clear, undeviating way: its follower acts in accordance with human nature and truth without contradiction among his acts. The rhetorical question therefore necessarily denies equality between the two.

In context, the parable concerns God and idols. Idols have neither power nor guidance for themselves or others, whereas God is straight in His essence and actions, guides creation to its assigned purposes, sends messengers, and legislates. Since His creation is not aimless and He guides every creature to its proper end, the parable also indicates the basis of prophethood and legislation while establishing monotheism.

Al-Mizan regards the explanation that it contrasts any source of good with what brings no good as too general, since the verse points specifically to the One inherently characterized by justice. It also rejects making its contextual subject merely the believer and disbeliever. Though its lexical wording can apply to them, or to one who commands justice and one who is silent, the surrounding enumeration of blessings and argument for monotheism confines its intended application to God and what is worshipped besides Him.
verses.77:
Al-Mizan explains that the Unseen and the witnessed are relative terms: a thing may be hidden in one respect and manifest in another. “The Unseen of the heavens and the earth” is best understood as what is within them but hidden from understanding, rather than something outside their limits. The Hour belongs to this Unseen because God counts it among the Unseen and because it is the day on which realities now concealed in this world become manifest. God’s possession of this Unseen is real dominion over a concrete reality, not merely knowledge of it.

The statement that the Unseen belongs to God is therefore the premise for the Hour’s ease. The Hour is a present but hidden reality of the heavens and earth, under God’s dominion just as their visible aspect is; He may keep it concealed and reveal it when He wills. The verse does not seek to establish that resurrection exists or is possible, but to deny that bringing it about is difficult. Its comparison with the twinkling of an eye gives listeners an image of the quickest and lightest human act; “or even swifter” means that, in reality, the divine command is more immediate still. Though the Hour is momentous for creation, it is no burden to God.

God’s power, unlike human power, is not conditioned by external means, accessible materials, bodily instruments, obstacles, or other circumstances. It is inherent in His necessary being and encompasses everything equally: no object is nearer or farther, easier or harder for Him. Differences in difficulty belong to things themselves and to their causal relations, not to divine power. Since everything depends on God for its existence, there can be no independent third factor limiting His power or sharing influence with Him. Causes, conditions, and impediments limit things in relation to one another, but not the all-encompassing divine power that acts upon each thing together with all its determinations and connections.

The verse thus shows that resurrection is the disclosure of realities after concealment, that God’s power embraces all things without distinction of ease or difficulty, and that existents are interconnected under a single power with no other influence. Al-Mizan notes a simpler causal perspective in which things appear separate and some depend on others, producing sequence, intermediaries, ease, and difficulty; but this does not qualify the preceding account of absolute power.

The commentary rejects the common interpretation that “To Allah belongs the Unseen” has an omitted word, “knowledge,” because knowledge alone has no evident connection with the immediate ease of the Hour and makes the clause a digression. It likewise rejects equating God’s dominion over the Unseen with His knowledge of unknown present and future matters, since this leaves that connection unresolved. Finally, it finds insufficient the claim that omnipotence means only that God can establish the Hour in the shortest time: the verse affirms that no real difference of difficulty exists for His absolute power.
verses.78:
Al-Mizan explains ummahāt as the plural of umm, “mother,” and afʾida as the sparse plural of fuʾād, meaning heart or understanding. The verse says that human beings are born without acquired knowledge, which they subsequently obtain through the senses, imagination, and intellect. In this respect, the human soul is initially like a blank slate.

This absence of knowledge concerns things other than oneself, not self-awareness. Mystics do not count awareness of oneself as “knowing something”; those reduced in old age to knowing nothing after knowledge (16:70) still remain aware of themselves. Thus the commentator rejects the claim that presential self-knowledge arises only after birth and maintains that the verse concerns ordinary acquired knowledge. Hearing and sight are especially primary among the external sources of perception, while the heart is the source of belief and thought; God grants these faculties so that people may give thanks.
verses.79:
Al-Mizan, citing al-Ṭabrisī, explains jaww al-samāʾ as the air distant from the earth: birds are disposed (musakhkharāt) in that expanse, and none sustains them except Allah. This exclusive attribution does not deny natural causes. God has granted existence both to birds and to the immediate causes of their flight, as well as to the relation between those causes and flight. A natural cause does not independently bestow existence on its effect; rather, the effect receives existence from God while depending on its cause having received existence from Him. Thus God alone is the real cause, even where proximate natural causes operate.

The term musakhkharāt itself implies natural causality, for disposal is the compelling of a cause to act as the disposer wills. The verse therefore expresses Qur’anic monotheism, not a rejection of causal relations. Bird-flight is no more extraordinary in itself than a human being standing on earth; familiarity merely dulls wonder. Yet the seeming exception of a heavy bird flying prompts inquiry into its cause, and the Qur’an uses such observable phenomena as arguments. Birds’ varied fluttering, gliding, wingless motion, stopping, hovering, ascent, and descent are all signs for those who have faith.
verses.80:
Al-Mizan explains that God has made settled homes a sakan, a place of residence and rest, and has made portable dwellings from tanned cattle skins: tents light enough to be used both on the day of travel (ẓaʿn) and on the day of halt. Bayt can denote whatever shelters a person at night, including dwellings of stone, clay, wool, or fur.

God has also provided wool from sheep, awbār from camels, and hair from goats, from which people make aḥthāth, abundant household furnishings, and matāʿ, the more general necessities and wares of life. These provisions display divine care in making human life manageable through varied homes and materials. The phrase “for a while” may indicate the transience of such blessings and warn the wise not to exchange the enduring joys of the hereafter for perishable comforts.
verses.81:
Al-Mizan explains that shade is linked to “what He created” because shade is itself an absence, existing consequentially through something else. Yet it is a great divine blessing: without the shade of night, trees, or plants, no living creature could survive. The retreats (aknān) in the mountains are their caves and hollows, for kann denotes what covers or shelters something.

The garments that protect from heat also protect from cold. Al-Ṭabrisī, reporting from ʿAtāʾ, explains the specific mention of heat by the greater need of the Hijaz’s inhabitants for protection from it; Arabs may mention one of two inseparable things while implying the other. Another possible explanation is that humanity first inhabited warmer regions and was especially exposed to intense heat. The garments protecting from violence are apparently armor of iron and similar materials.

By enumerating shade, shelter, clothing, and armor, God shows the completion of His blessing so that people will submit to their Benefactor, abandon arrogance, and recognize that His favors are intended for their good.
verses.82: Al-Mizan explains al-balāgh al-mubīn as clear communication; balāgh is a noun, while tablīgh is its verbal noun. After recounting divine blessings and establishing the argument for monotheism in lordship, prophethood, and resurrection, the verse reproaches and threatens those who turn away. The Prophet’s task is only to convey God’s message plainly, without ambiguity or concealment. The call seeks people’s welfare in this world and the next and does not coerce them; if they reject it, a messenger has no further duty. The verse also consoles the Prophet.
verses.83:
Al-Mizan holds that they “recognize” God’s blessing as coming from Him, but then deny it chiefly in practice: instead of believing in God, His Messenger, and the Hereafter and submitting accordingly, they act as deniers. Verbal denial despite prior recognition is also possible, but the preferred sense is practical denial. “Most of them are the faithless” indicates that most are entrenched in complete disbelief, obstinacy, and obstruction of God’s way, beyond mere failure to act on what they recognize.

The commentary rejects explanations that “most” excludes people against whom the proof was not established, for the verse concerns only those who recognize the blessing and then deny it; the blessing they recognize is itself the proof. It also finds unsupported the claim that “most” refers to those who would not later believe, and regards as unusual Ḥasan al-Baṣrī’s reported view that “most” means all.

The verse also refutes the Determinists’ claim that disbelievers receive no divine favors. Blessing has two aspects: a creational blessing suited to bodily well-being, and a legislative blessing that leads to recognition of God, His Messenger, and the Hereafter and is used in a manner pleasing to God. Believers enjoy both; disbelievers in this world receive the former but are deprived of the latter.
verses.84:
Al-Mizan takes the day on which a witness is raised from every nation to be the Day of Judgment. These witnesses testify to the realities of their communities’ deeds. The verse does not establish that every witness must be a prophet; the witness may be another person, such as an Imam, and “every nation” may mean the people living in the era of each witness.

The disbelievers are denied permission to speak or offer excuses while the witnesses testify against their communities. More broadly, they cannot use speech or stratagem to repel the evil of that Day or repair their corrupted worldly deeds. Rectification would require either forgiveness or a return to earthly life for righteous action: the denial of permission blocks the former, and “nor shall they be allowed to make amends” blocks the latter. They are not summoned to please God by correcting the past, because the Hereafter is the abode of recompense and punishment, not action, and no return to the world is possible.
verses.85: Al-Mizan distinguishes the punishment of the Day of Judgment from worldly punishments. Worldly penalties may be lightened or postponed, whereas, once the wrongdoers have been reckoned with, sentenced, and brought near enough to see the fire, the punishment of the Hereafter is neither reduced nor delayed. Calling them “wrongdoers,” rather than merely disbelievers, indicates the basis of this judgment.
verses.86:
Al-Mizan explains that alladhīna ashrakū denotes idolaters and polytheists, and that “their partners” are the beings whom they falsely ascribed as partners to God. They are called the polytheists’ partners, rather than God’s partners, because they possess no real partnership with Him. Interpretations that make them financial partners or devils sharing in the polytheists’ possessions, offspring, disbelief, or its consequences are rejected.

On the Day of Judgment, the polytheists identify these alleged partners before God in a desperate attempt to save themselves. Their partners then reject their claim and call them liars. This rejection is elsewhere described as the alleged partners’ disbelief in having been associated with God.
verses.87:
Al-Mizan explains alqaw ilā Allāh yawma-idhin al-salam as the polytheists’ submission and surrender to God on the Day of Judgment, apparently under compulsion by His power. It is not merely the disclosure of God’s oneness: knowing the truth differs from submitting and believing in it. Human happiness depends on voluntary submission and faith with their consequences, and the arena for such choice is this world, the abode of action, not the Hereafter, the abode of recompense.

Although the polytheists had certainty of the truth in this world, they arrogantly preferred worship and submission to their alleged associates. In the Hereafter they see God as the manifest truth, are surrounded by torment, and submit unwillingly. Such compelled submission does not benefit them. Their fabricated claims and the supposed divinity of their associates vanish when those associates deny them, leaving only God, to whom they submit reluctantly.
verses.88: Al-Mizan applies the verse particularly to the leaders of disbelief. In addition to the punishment shared by wrongdoers and disbelievers, those who obstinately disbelieved and barred others from God’s way receive an added punishment for that obstruction. Their corruption principally consists in preventing people from following God’s path; it may also refer to the social corruption resulting from preventing the establishment of a righteous society that those people would have formed had they accepted the religion.
verses.89:
Al-Mizan explains that the raising of a witness from every nation on the Day of Judgment is distinct from the general resurrection for reckoning: one witness is raised from among each community to testify to its deeds, thereby completing the proof and eliminating excuses. The earlier occurrence of this phrase introduced the disbelievers’ inability to speak; here it introduces the Prophet’s testimony.

All the evidences of that Day—witnesses, gathering, questioning, the scale, and reckoning—must establish the reality of each person’s good and evil deeds and yield an incontrovertible judgment of happiness or misery. Therefore, a witness cannot give merely compelled, fabricated, second-hand, or conjectural testimony, even though God has power to compel such testimony. That would not be a conclusive proof fitting a Day on which truth and reality prevail. The required witness must be divinely protected from falsehood, know the true inward as well as outward reality of the deeds in question, and testify through direct observation. “From among themselves” indicates this direct witnessing, rather than reliance on rational or transmitted evidence, as illustrated by Jesus’ statement, “I was a witness over them as long as I was among them, but when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them, and You are Witness to all things” (5:117).

The commentary consequently reads “nation” as the community of a particular era, including disbelievers as well as believers, and the community to which Muḥammad was sent as many such temporal communities. Each has its own witness, who may be a prophet or someone else; witnessing and prophethood are not identical, as indicated by “And (He will bring forth) the prophets and the witnesses... (39:69).” The witness must be one appointed to observe the people and endowed with divine infallibility.

Although some scholars take “these” in “We shall bring you as a witness against these” to mean all the people to whom Muḥammad was sent, Al-Mizan holds that it means the witnesses themselves. Those witnesses testify concerning the people, while the Prophet testifies concerning the witnesses, verifying their status rather than directly observing the actions of every community. He therefore need not be contemporaneous with every witness. This reading reconciles the present verse with “Thus We have made you a just community that you will be witnesses over the people and the Messenger will be a witness over you” (2:143), and prevents the conflicts produced by treating the Prophet as the direct witness over every individual or by restricting the witnessed nation to believers alone.

The Book’s being a clarification (tibyān) of all things ordinarily means that, as a book of guidance, it clarifies everything needed for guidance: true knowledge of the origin and end of the cosmos, virtuous ethics, divine laws, pious accounts, and moral admonitions. It does not mean that its lexical wording expounds every field of human knowledge. For those who submit, it is specifically guidance to the straight path, divine mercy leading to worldly and heavenly good and to God’s reward and pleasure, and good news of forgiveness, divine satisfaction, and eternal bliss. Traditions stating that the Qur’an contains knowledge of what has been, what is, and what will be until the Day of Judgment, if correct, show that tibyān extends beyond ordinary lexical signification and may include indications of hidden realities inaccessible to conventional understanding.

Al-Mizan further judges from the context of monotheism, prophethood, and resurrection that “We have sent down the Book” is not an independent statement, but a circumstantial clause connected with “We shall bring you as a witness.” Although grammarians dispute a circumstantial clause beginning with a perfect verb, some posit an implicit qad. The meaning is that God made Muḥammad a witness after having revealed to him, in this world, a Book that distinguishes truth from falsehood; by it he testifies against the wrongdoers for their oppression and for the Muslims’ submission, while serving as their guide, mercy, and bearer of good news. The association of the Book with testimony in “And the earth will shine with the light of its Lord, and the Book will be set in place, and the prophets and the witnesses will be brought” (39:69) supports this connection. Al-Mizan says that this Book is the Preserved Tablet, of which the Qur’an is a part, and that, though the Tablet’s testimony differs from the Prophet’s, both depend ultimately on the decree of the revealed Book.
verses.90:
Al-Mizan presents the verse’s commands—justice, iḥsān, and giving to relatives—as foundations of a sound human society, on which individual happiness depends. Islamic teachings therefore seek to establish their doctrines and laws as social realities, including through the communal character of worship.

Justice (ʿadl) is fairness, the opposite of oppression. Al-Rāghib distinguishes intellectually apprehended ʿadl from terms used for tangible equivalence, and distinguishes an absolute rational justice from a law-defined justice that may be abrogated, such as retribution. In the present verse, justice is equivalence in recompense: good is repaid with good and evil with its like, whereas benevolence repays good with more and evil with less. More fundamentally, justice is balance and the avoidance of excess and deficiency: everything receives its due and is put in its proper place. Thus, it means affirming truth in belief, pursuing one’s well-being rather than desire in personal conduct, and, socially, assigning people their due places, rewarding and punishing rightly, vindicating the oppressed, and applying law impartially. Justice is consequently inseparable from goodness. Al-Mizan qualifies al-Rāghib’s description of retaliatory punishment as “evil” or “aggression”: it is so from the wrongdoer’s standpoint, but is moderation and goodness when it administers justice.

Although justice is general, the context particularly concerns social justice. The command addresses individuals while making the community, especially its governing authority, responsible for its realization. Here iḥsān means voluntarily initiating benefit for others, not merely performing an act well or giving recompense. By relieving poverty and adversity and spreading compassion, it also circulates wealth, security, and affection through society.

Giving to dhū al-qurbā means sharing wealth with relatives, a special emphasis on the family unit from which wider civil society develops. The wording can indicate the class of all relatives. However, exegetical traditions attributed to the Imāms of Ahl al-Bayt interpret “the relatives” as the Imām from the lineage of Prophet Muḥammad and the giving as the allocation of khums under Know that whatever thing you may come by, a fifth of it is for Allah and the M essenger, for the relatives and the orphans, for the needy and the traveller (8:41). The singular dhū al-qurbā, unlike the plurals in other verses, may support this reading; and its singularity in 8:41, alongside plural “orphans” and “needy,” weakens the likelihood that it merely denotes a general class. The verse itself contains no clear indication that ītāʾ has the same meaning as iḥsān, or that iḥsān simply means kindness in general.

Faḥshāʾ comprises abhorrent words and deeds and apparently denotes exceeding proper bounds; munkar is what society rejects for its ugliness or sinfulness; and baghī is unjust aggression against others, though the term can have other uses. Their instances may overlap, but each is separately prohibited because such conduct severs social harmony, corrupts society inwardly, and destroys individual happiness. The prohibition therefore calls for a community in which rights are respected, oppression and ugly conduct disappear, and mercy, love, harmony, strength, and stability replace hostility and division. The concluding admonition calls people to recognize that these commands are their life and happiness.
verses.91:
Al-Mizan explains ʿahd as preserving and caring for something over time, and hence as a binding agreement requiring observance. “Allah’s covenant” apparently concerns a covenant specifically made with God, not every agreement in general.

The prohibited oaths are solemn, deliberate oaths sworn by God, not frivolous expressions such as casual “yes, by God” or “no, by God.” “Having made Allah a witness over yourselves” confirms that God is invoked as guarantor. Both violating a covenant and breaking such an oath are forbidden, but the latter is graver and receives special legal emphasis, particularly in judicial matters.

An oath binds a statement or undertaking to an entity of high sanctity. If the sworn report proves false, or the sworn undertaking is not fulfilled, this dishonours the One invoked, much as defaulting on a commitment dishonours valuable collateral. Breaking an oath sworn by God thus has a double fault: it violates the promise and disrespects God’s sanctity, severing the relation established through the oath. “Indeed Allah knows what you do” reinforces that this detested conduct is known to Him.
verses.92:
Al-Mizan explains the verse as an elaboration of the prohibition on breaking solemn oaths. Naqḍ is the undoing of something firmly bound, such as rope or spun yarn, and inkāthan similarly means unweaving; the image is therefore of a woman laboriously spinning yarn and then undoing it until it becomes useless. Dakhal denotes something introduced into another thing without becoming part of it and commonly conveys deceit or treachery.

Making oaths a means of deceit is to use them first to reassure others and then to betray them by breaking them, so that the oath-makers obtain greater worldly benefit than those to whom they swore. The phrase likens this conduct to undoing spun yarn and prohibits it. Some read “making your oaths” as an emphatic rhetorical question of disapproval.

“Allah only tests you thereby” means that this situation tests people’s deeds and choices. On the Day of Resurrection, God will disclose the matters over which they differed, exposing the real character of their worldly pursuits and their rejection of truth.
verses.93:
Al-Mizan explains that human differences neither frustrate God’s creative purpose nor lie outside His control: had He wished, He could have made all people one community. His guiding some and leading others astray, however, operates through the principle that happiness and misery rest on human choice. He has made known the way to ultimate happiness through obedience and to misery through disobedience; those who choose either course, including those who repent from sin, receive its corresponding requital.

The assurance that people will be questioned about what they did prevents the mistaken conclusion that divine guidance and misguidance abolish human choice or make prophethood meaningless. Human inclinations toward obedience or disobedience remain consequential, and God’s guidance or misguidance corresponds to them; all are answerable for their choices and acts.
verses.94:
Al-Mizan treats this as an independent, specific prohibition on using oaths deceptively, following the general prohibition on breaking them. Breaking an oath dishonours God, whom the swearer made witness; deceitful oaths add the social harm expressed by feet slipping after being firm, suffering punishment for barring from God’s way, and facing a great punishment.

A first breach can make oath-breaking seem trivial, turning swearing and breaking oaths into instruments of betrayal. This habituates a person to deceit, intrigue, lying, and corruption, until he becomes a source of social ruin and deviates from God’s path, which accords with sound human nature. The slipping foot metaphor signifies abandoning a firm commitment. Steadfastness and integrity in commitments are among the noblest qualities and foundations of virtue, and preserving oaths is one means of sustaining them.

Here ṣudūd means turning away from the natural and prophetic guidance to truthfulness, uprightness, fidelity to commitments, and freedom from deceit and corruption. “You suffer ill” means punishment and may indicate adverse consequences in this world, while the great punishment is assured in the hereafter. Deceitful oaths thus corrupt the earth after it has been set right.

Some scholars restrict the verse to breaking the early allegiance to Prophet Muḥammad, reading the slipping of feet as apostasy and ṣadd as preventing others from God’s religion. Al-Mizan finds that restriction unsupported by the general course of the passage; even if it was the occasion of revelation, the verse remains generally applicable.
verses.95: Al-Mizan takes the verse as a general prohibition on breaking any promise made in God’s name for worldly gain, reinforcing the preceding command to fulfil covenants. A thaman is what is given in exchange for something; thus, selling Allah’s covenant for a paltry gain is exchanging one’s pledged commitment for trivial worldly compensation. What is with Allah is better.
verses.96:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse grounds the claim that what is with Allah is better: all that belongs to this changing material world is transient and depleted, whereas what God has promised the righteous endures without perishing. Its general wording makes it a universal axiom.

The reward of the patient follows because fulfilling a covenant requires patience against the desire to break it when doing so seems advantageous. The promise extends from those patient in covenant-keeping to every patience for God’s sake: patience in obedience, refraining from sin, and enduring calamity.

“For the best of what they used to do” does not mean that God rewards only a believer’s best deeds while disregarding other good deeds, nor that it selects obligatory and recommended deeds over permissible deeds. The context concerns deeds connected with patience, and permissible acts have no necessary connection with it. Rather, God rewards each deed of the patient as the best instance of that kind: a patient believer’s prayer, for example, is recompensed as the best such prayer even if it was not actually so. Patience for God’s sake perfects deeds, so they are not scrutinized for features that would otherwise make them inferior; this accords with: Indeed the patient will be paid in full their reward without any reckoning (39:10).

The shift to “We will surely pay” returns to a direct divine mode after the preceding references to Allah in the third person. Al-Mizan explains that the intervening commands and prohibitions were attributed to divine majesty in the third person to reinforce their authority, while the return to the first person emphasizes the promise of recompense. A comparable combination of first- and third-person attribution occurs in: W hen We change a sign with another in its place—and Allah knows best what He sends down ….
verses.97:
Al-Mizan reads the verse as a promise that believing men and women who act righteously receive equally a good life and the best reward for their deeds. It thus gives women glad tidings that faith and righteous action are accepted from them without distinction from men, contrary to views that deprived women of spiritual merit or denied their elevation. Faith is a condition: the deeds of one without faith are futile.

“We shall revive him with a good life” grants a real, new mode of life, not merely an improvement in ordinary life or a metaphor. The wording speaks of giving life, not simply making an existing life pleasant, and parallels the life and light by which a person walks among people. Its light is knowledge that guides to truth in belief and action; with it comes a distinct capacity to revive truth and dispel falsehood.

This life enables the believer to distinguish enduring truth from passing falsehood, turn from the deceptive attractions of the world, and remain free from Satan’s whispering, desire, and worldly allurements. His heart attaches only to God: he seeks His countenance and nearness, fears only His displeasure and distance, and sees disobedience as the only ugliness God has declared reprehensible. He consequently experiences inner brilliance, perfection, strength, dignity, joy, and a life of enduring blessing without misery. These are real effects of life and establish that the promised life is genuine.

It is distinct from common life in degree, not as a separate life alongside it; the person is not multiplied. Like the Holy Spirit (Rūḥ al-Quddus) granted to prophets, it elevates a person without changing his identity. Its description as ṭayyib means that it is free from internal corruption and harmful effects.

Al-Mizan rejects interpretations that identify the good life merely with Paradise, Barzakh, worldly contentment with provision, lawful provision, or daily sustenance. The reward “by the best of what they used to do” has the meaning previously explained: the patient believer’s deeds are rewarded as the best instance of their kind.
verses.98: Al-Mizan explains the command as seeking God’s protection from Satan’s misguidance while reciting the Qurʾan; it concerns the reader’s inward state during recitation. Saying ‘I seek refuge in God from Satan, the accursed’ (aʿūdhu bi-Allāh min al-Shayṭān al-rajīm), or a similar formula, is only a means of evoking this inward refuge and is not effective by itself. The command is to seek refuge in God, not merely to pronounce a formula. Accordingly, interpreting “when you recite” as merely intending to recite is an overly loose reading.
verses.99:
Al-Mizan makes the verse the reason for seeking refuge during Qurʾan recitation: Satan has no authority over those who believe and rely on their Lord. Seeking refuge is itself a form of trust in God, since trust replaces refuge in the explanation of Satan’s lack of authority.

Faith together with reliance on God constitutes true divine servanthood. The verse thus accords with: Indeed as for M y servants you do not have any authority over them, except the perverse who follow you, (15:42). To entrust one’s affairs to another and submit to that one’s influence is a particular manifestation of servitude.
verses.100:
Al-Mizan explains that Satan’s authority is confined to those who take him as guardian, let him manage their affairs, and obey him, and to those who make him a partner. Since obedience resembles worship, taking as an ally one whom God has not authorized as an ally amounts to associating a partner with God and worshipping another.

There is therefore no middle position between reliance on God and alliance with Satan and his worship: whoever does not rely on God belongs among Satan’s allies. A proposed reading takes the singular pronoun in “those who make him a partner” as referring to God, making Satan’s authority extend separately to polytheists and monotheists who ally with Satan. Al-Mizan finds this unpersuasive because it requires an unexplained shift in the pronoun.
verses.101:
Al-Mizan understands the verse to concern abrogation (naskh) and to answer the polytheists’ charge that the Prophet Muḥammad was a fabricator. The Jews especially denied abrogation, and the polytheists may have acquired this objection from them. Baddalnā means placing one thing in another’s place, more broadly than exchange for compensation. Thus, when God changes a sign with another in its place, He puts the second verse in place of the first, leaving the substituted verse as the operative one.

“Allah knows best what He sends down” is a parenthetical assertion that revelation remains in its proper place because its Sender knows its nature best. The polytheists regarded replacing one statement with another as inconsistent with divine dignity and consequently called the Prophet not merely fabricating in this instance, but altogether “a fabricator.” Since his message as a whole was attributed to God, they reasoned that fabrication in one part would invalidate all of it.

The majority do not understand the wisdom of abrogation: divine rulings rest on human welfare, and because circumstances and benefits change, a prior ruling may have to be replaced by one suited to the new condition. A minority may know this but reject the truth arrogantly and contentiously.
verses.102:
Al-Mizan explains that the Holy Spirit (Rūḥ al-Quddus) is a spirit purified from material impurity, error, fault, and misguidance. Other passages call it the Trustworthy Spirit (al-Rūḥ al-Amīn) and identify the bringer of revelation as Gabriel; the verse therefore indicates the Qurʾan’s gradual revelation through Gabriel. “From your Lord,” rather than “my Lord,” expresses God’s special care and mercy for the Prophet Muḥammad and indicates that he is commanded to inform his hearers of this fact, not merely repeat words.

The pronoun in “has brought it down” apparently refers first to the Qurʾan as the abrogating verse, though it may refer to the Qurʾan generally. Nazzala-hu, rather than anzala-hu, suggests gradual sending down. The revelation fortifies believers, especially through its renewal of rulings as benefits change. A believer who continues on an earlier instruction after the direction required by the underlying benefit has changed will have his faith weakened; a new command directing him toward the true benefit instead increases his steadfastness. Abrogation therefore gives believers stability upon stability.

Guidance and good news are for those who submit their judgment to God without objection: an abrogating verse gives them a new path and the promise of happiness and Paradise. The differing descriptions reflect the distinction between imān and islām. Faith resides in the heart and gives stability in knowledge and consent, while submission appears in outward compliance, is guided to required deeds, and receives the glad tidings of the final happiness.
verses.103:
Al-Mizan explains the accusation as the claim that Prophet Muḥammad learned his message from a non-Arab man with some knowledge of religion and prophethood, then falsely presented it as revelation. The contrast between that man’s non-Arabic tongue and the Qurʾan’s clear Arabic answers the charge only if it concerns the Qurʾan’s exact wording. It does not by itself exclude the possibility that the man taught concepts which the Prophet then eloquently rendered in Arabic; “teaches” more naturally concerns meanings than dictated wording.

Accordingly, the response is completed by the following verses. If the allegation concerns the words, a non-Arabic speaker could not have produced this clear Arabic Qurʾan. If it concerns the meanings, the Qurʾan contains true knowledge accepted by sound reason, and God guided the Prophet to it. As a believer in God’s signs, he would not falsely attribute knowledge to God; fabrication against Him belongs only to those who disbelieve in His signs. The Qurʾan is thus neither fabricated nor taken from a human source and falsely ascribed to God.
verses.104:
Al-Mizan explains these verses as completing the answer to the charge that another person taught Prophet Muḥammad the Qurʾan’s meanings and that he falsely attributed them to God. Those who disbelieve in God’s signs are not guided to their manifest, true knowledge and face a painful punishment. Since the Prophet is guided by God and believes in His signs, he cannot be among those who fabricate lies against God; such persistent lying belongs to the unbelievers. The verses therefore establish that he does not fabricate.

Some commentators detach these verses from the preceding accusation, take the preceding verse as a complete appeal to a supposed linguistic miracle, and read these verses only as a threat against the accusers. Al-Mizan rejects this approach: the preceding verse merely states that the Qurʾan is clear Arabic, which the non-Arabic man could not produce, and does not itself assert a linguistic miracle. Detaching the verses consequently fails to answer the objection at its root.
verses.105:
Al-Mizan explains these verses as completing the answer to the charge that another person taught Prophet Muḥammad the Qurʾan’s meanings and that he falsely attributed them to God. Those who disbelieve in God’s signs are not guided to their manifest, true knowledge and face a painful punishment. verses.106:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse conditionally threatens God’s wrath and a great punishment for whoever renounces faith after believing. Muṭmaʾinn denotes tranquillity, calmness, and stability, while sharḥ means expansion; to “open up their breasts to unfaith” is therefore to receive and embrace disbelief willingly and completely.

The exception concerns one compelled to utter or outwardly display disbelief while the heart remains at rest in faith, since coercion cannot make the heart accept disbelief. The following clause corrects and completes the meaning of the condition: the threatened apostasy is not outward speech under compulsion, but voluntary inward acceptance of unbelief. This explains why the exception occurs between the condition and its consequence.

Al-Mizan mentions an alternative grammatical reading that treats “Whoever renounces faith” as a permutation of the preceding description of those who deny God’s signs, and makes “but those who open up their breasts to unfaith” a new statement. It rejects this explanation as unnecessary and plainly absurd.
verses.107: Al-Mizan explains that God’s wrath and the great punishment befall them because they preferred the worldly life—devoted to animalistic pleasure and personal desire—to the eternal Hereafter, life in proximity to the Lord of the Worlds and humanity’s final goal. Seeking a worldly life detached from the Hereafter amounts to disbelieving in it. God does not guide such faithless people; deprived of guidance, they stray from happiness, Paradise, and divine pleasure into wrath and punishment.
verses.108:
Al-Mizan explains that those who choose the worldly life over the Hereafter and are deprived of divine guidance are the ones whose hearts, hearing, and sight God has sealed, and who are heedless. Having made the material world their sole end, they sever their connection with the Hereafter. Their senses and intellect remain confined to this world: they cannot perceive what should be learned, heed admonition, or understand proofs that would guide them to the Hereafter.

Their impervious hearts, ears, and eyes are the divine seal, while their obliviousness to the Hereafter is heedlessness. The preceding deprivation of guidance, resulting from attachment to the world, identifies the sealing and heedlessness meant here. The sealing is attributed to God as retribution, whereas heedlessness is their own trait.
verses.109: Al-Mizan explains that they are losers in the Hereafter because they spent their capital in the worldly life and retain no provision for the life to come. A similar statement occurs in Surah Hud: Undoubtedly, they are the ones who will be the biggest losers in the Hereafter (11:22); its stronger emphasis may be due to their additional trait of obstructing God’s path.
verses.110:
Al-Mizan explains that fitna, from which futinū derives, originally meant testing gold by fire and was later extended to every trial or torture. The Quraysh and Meccan polytheists tortured believers in order to make them renounce their religion; some died under torture, including ʿAmmār’s parents. ʿAmmār outwardly renounced faith under duress, establishing taqiyya, and the verse is consequently linked to the exception for one compelled while his heart remains at rest in faith.

The verse promises forgiveness and mercy on the Day of Judgement to those who emigrated after persecution, then strove and remained patient, in contrast to the complete loss threatened to others. Its concluding repetition, “indeed, after that, your Lord will surely be all-forgiving, all-merciful,” confirms and summarizes this promise. Migration alone is insufficient, and neither is migration accepted without subsequent striving in God’s path and patience; all these conditions are integral to divine pleasure.
verses.111:
Al-Mizan explains that every soul’s “coming” on the Day of Judgement means its appearance before the Divine Judge. In “for itself” (ʿan nafsi-hā), nafs first means the human person, while the second use is emphatic, meaning the soul itself; the pronoun avoids repeating the noun.

Each soul will be present for reckoning and plead in its own defence, seeking to justify itself with every excuse. Having formerly concerned itself with everything but itself, it then realizes that it has no real concern beyond itself. No soul will defend another or be concerned with another.

Tawfiya, “recompense in full,” means receiving one’s full due without reduction. Since each soul is recompensed for precisely what it has done, the recompense is the deed itself, without alteration or substitution. There is therefore neither addition nor diminution in what is deserved, and no injustice. Pleading cannot avert the recompense earned, because the relation between the deed and its recompense cannot be changed.
verses.112:
Al-Mizan explains this as a general parable of a town granted complete material security: safety from danger, settled tranquillity without flight or dispersal, and raghadan, abundant, comfortable provision from every direction without the hardship of seeking it. The next verse adds the spiritual favour of a messenger sent from among its people to guide their worldly and otherworldly welfare.

Their ingratitude for these blessings and denial of the messenger turned the blessings into punishment. Although al-Ṭabrisī in Majmaʿ al-Bayān attributes an application to Mecca, afflicted with seven years of famine, to Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Qatāda, the context indicates that the verse is a general parable and prepares for the ensuing discussion of lawful and unlawful food and the prohibition against inventing such rulings without divine authority.

The phrase fa-adhāqa-hā Allāh libās al-jawʿ wa al-khawf conveys both that they were made to “taste” a measure of hunger and fear—implying God’s power to increase it beyond measure—and that these afflictions enveloped them as libās, clothing envelops the body. The ending, “because of what they used to do,” confirms the established divine recompense for gratitude and ingratitude.
verses.113: Al-Mizan regards the messenger sent from among the town’s own people as its added spiritual blessing, complementing its material blessings. He was sent to improve their worldly and afterlife condition and to warn them against ingratitude; yet they denied the known messenger and his guidance. Their denial was wrongdoing, so punishment seized them for that injustice.
verses.114:
Al-Mizan takes the command to eat what God provides as lawful and good, and to give thanks, as the conclusion drawn from the preceding parable: punishment followed ingratitude for provision and rejection of guidance. The verse concerns all God-given sustenance that is ḥalāl and ṭayyib, not specifically war-spoils; the latter interpretation lacks textual support.

Religious lawfulness rests on natural permissibility, since religion accords with human nature. God has made particular plant and animal substances fit for nourishment and naturally acceptable rather than repugnant, and these are lawful to eat. The command to eat introduces the command to gratitude, because a blessing by its nature calls for thanks.

The phrase “if it is Him that you worship” addresses believers and stresses exclusive worship of God. Al-Mizan rejects the view that it addresses polytheists by treating worship as mere obedience, or as worship of God through idols: no contextual indication supports this, and polytheists neither worship God in this way nor regard idol-worship as His worship. Accordingly, the parable and the surrounding legislative address are directed to believers; extending the address to everyone is possible but strained.
verses.115: Al-Mizan notes that the Qur’an repeats this ruling in both early and late Meccan sūrahs and among the first and last Medinan revelations. Though the verse has been taken to limit forbidden foods to carrion, blood, swine-flesh, and what has been offered to other than Allah, these are the principal Qur’anic prohibitions. Other food prohibitions were established by the Prophet Muḥammad under his Lord’s command, as supported by: Take whatever the Messenger gives you, and relinquish whatever he forbids you (59:7). The exception remains for one compelled without rebellion or aggression.
verses.116:
Al-Mizan interprets the verse as forbidding people to declare things lawful or unlawful merely by verbal assertion and thereby fabricate lies against God. In its context, addressed either to believers or to all people, it prohibits religious and social innovations introduced without revelation: adding something to religion is lying about God even when one does not explicitly attribute it to Him.

The commentary rejects the common restriction of the verse to polytheists’ food practices, such as permitting carrion, blood, and offerings to other gods or prohibiting the Bāḥira and Sāʾiba, because the context does not sustain it. Those who invent lies against Allah cannot be felicitous, a point the following verse explains.
verses.117:
Al-Mizan reads verses (16:117-118) as answering an implicit objection arising from the limitation of Qur’anic food prohibitions: if other things are permissible, why were certain good things forbidden to the Jews? The earlier account is apparently that in: To the Jews We forbade every animal having an undivided hoof … (6:146).

Those restrictions were not injustice. Things originally lawful were forbidden to the Children of Israel as punishment for their own wrongdoing and disobedience, as stated in: Due to the wrongdoing of the Jews, We prohibited them certain good things that were permitted to them (4:160). Had they returned and repented, God would have accepted their repentance, removed the restrictions, and restored what had been forbidden. Thus the passage continues the discourse on lawful and unlawful and leads into the promise of forgiveness for those who repent.

verses.119:
Al-Mizan explains bi-jahāla not as ignorance of a ruling or of the act’s subject, but as failure to realize fully the reality of a sin. A person may know that an act is forbidden and remain accountable, yet, overcome by desire, act without contemplating its true evil; with full realization, he would not have committed it. Mere unawareness would not be a sin requiring repentance and forgiveness.

The verse completes the explanation that the Children of Israel wronged themselves through sin and persistence, and that their restrictions were not divine injustice. Nevertheless, forgiveness and mercy remain open to those who commit evil in this sense, then repent and reform. Reform demonstrates that repentance is real and stable rather than empty; forgiveness and mercy follow repentance itself, while reform clarifies its genuineness. The concluding repetition—“indeed, after that, your Lord”—summarizes the preceding condition and emphasizes the care attached to forgiveness after repentance.
verses.120:
Al-Mizan presents the verses on Abraham as explaining the contrast between restrictions imposed on the Children of Israel and the religion revealed to the Prophet. This religion is Abraham’s balanced, nature-conforming faith: it permits good things, forbids vile things, and brings its followers the benefits it brought Abraham in this world and the next.

“Abraham was a nation” means that he stood alone as a community in worship, akin to a person being a tribe unto himself; related explanations call him an exemplary leader or the sole monotheist of his time. Qānitan li Allāh means continuously obeying and worshipping God. A ḥanīf is one who turns away from extremes toward moderation and balance, and Abraham was not among the polytheists.
verses.121: Al-Mizan explains ijtabāʾ as God’s special choice of Abraham, preserving him from deviation in belief. The sequence—Abraham’s gratitude followed by God’s choice—indicates that he was chosen because he was grateful for divine blessings. This supports the view that the essence of gratitude is sincerity in servitude, as in: You will not find most of them to be grateful (7:17).
verses.122: Al-Mizan interprets the good (ḥasana) given to Abraham in this world as a good life, including wealth and great respect, while in the Hereafter he is among the Righteous. God’s choosing is guidance, and the Straight Path bears the meaning explained at Guide us to the Straight Path (1:6). Abraham’s attributes indicate the gifts of this upright religion: whoever adopts it will be led to what it led him to.
verses.123: Al-Mizan says that the command to follow Abraham’s creed emphasizes his inclination toward truth as a ḥanīf and his complete rejection of polytheism.
verses.124:
Al-Mizan explains sabt as involving cessation from work, whether it denotes the Sabbath day itself or the prescribed abstention from work on it. The Sabbath was exclusively legislated for the Israelites: they were required to cease work one day a week and dedicate it to worship, just as Muslims have Friday for communal worship and prayer.

The use of ʿalā in “prescribed for” conveys an imposed duty, intensification, and trial rather than a benefit. The Sabbath was therefore a burden placed upon them, one that eventually led to curses and transformation for some. The most fitting meaning of “those who differed about it” is that they differed after it was legislated: some accepted it, some rejected it, and some hypocritically sought to evade it while outwardly accepting it. God will judge them over this disagreement on the Day of Resurrection.

The commentary rejects explanations that make their disagreement precede the Sabbath’s imposition—such as their allegedly choosing Saturday over Friday—as well as readings that take “differed” simply to mean disobeyed or posit disagreement over an undesignated day of assembly. Such views, often based on reports, do not fully fit the wording.

The verse answers the question raised by the special laws imposed on the Israelites and their abrogation: the Sabbath was a test imposed because of their repeated disobedience, not a law instituted for their benefit. It is an appendix to the preceding sequence about Jewish restrictions and Abraham’s creed, whereas “Invite to the way of your Lord …” begins a new discourse. Its placement is thus not a disconnection between the command to follow Abraham and the command to invite to God’s way.
verses.125:
Al-Mizan understands wisdom (ḥikma), good advice (mawʿiẓa ḥasana), and disputation in the best manner (jādil-hum billatī hiya aḥsan) as methods for inviting people to God’s way. Wisdom attains truth through knowledge and reason and provides an unambiguous demonstration; advice softens the heart through beneficial exposition, lessons, praise, and good effects; and disputation uses argument to turn an opponent from insistence and contention. They correspond to demonstration (burhān), rhetoric (khaṭāba), and dialectic (jidāl).

Advice must be good and disputation must be the best, since neither every admonition nor every argument serves truth. God knows those astray and guided, and knows that only these modes benefit His way, which is true belief and righteous action. Advice by one who disregards it calls in practice to its opposite. Likewise, arguing for truth through false premises accepted by an opponent promotes falsehood and so extinguishes truth, unless those premises are used to expose the opponent’s falsehood.

Good advice requires that the adviser heed it personally and use praiseworthy conduct that makes hearts receptive. The best disputation avoids provoking obstinacy, false premises except for contradiction, bad expression, disparagement of the opponent or what they hold sacred, insult, and every ignorant manner. Such conduct would seek to revive truth through falsehood. Disputation demands a higher excellence than advice: all wisdom is permitted, only good advice, and only the best kind of disputation.

The verse does not assign each method exclusively to a particular class of people, nor require all three for every recipient. Depending on the circumstance and the aim of making truth effective, one, two, or all three may be used. Thus the view that wisdom belongs only to intellectual elites, advice to the common people, and disputation to obstinate opponents has some subtlety but no decisive textual basis; any group may benefit from the other methods. Nor is best disputation outside invitation merely because it can expose fallacy: dialectic may use accepted premises without that being its sole aim, and both argument and refutation can invite people, though their contentious form accounts for the shift in expression.
verses.126:
Al-Mizan explains muʿāqaba as retaliation or equivalent recompense: bringing an unpleasant consequence upon someone after the harm they caused. The verse addresses Muslims concerning retaliation against polytheists and disbelievers who punished them for faith in God and rejection of idols. Retaliation is permitted only to the measure of what they suffered.

Yet patient endurance without retribution is better for those who are patient, because it prefers God’s pleasure and reward in trial over the desire for vengeance. Forgiveness and pardon are acts of noble character and yield beautiful consequences for the one who practices them.
verses.127: Al-Mizan takes this as a command to the Prophet Muḥammad to endure hardship, coupled with reassurance that patience is possible only through God’s power and strengthening. Since God commands him to be patient, He has empowered him for it. He is also told not to grieve over the disbelievers because of their disbelief, nor to be distressed by their scheming, apparently either at present or continually rather than only in the future.
verses.128:
Al-Mizan explains that both Godwariness and virtue independently bring divine support and thwart the plots of the religion’s enemies. The verse therefore explains why the Prophet need not be distressed by their guile and promises victory.

The commentary notes that the final verses resemble Medinan material more than Meccan material. Reports from both Sunnī and Shīʿa sources say that they were revealed as the Prophet Muḥammad returned from Uḥud, though these reports are to be discussed separately. While the verses can be connected to what precedes, the prior verse accords more closely with the chapter’s central purpose; apart from certain exceptions, the chapter otherwise follows a single connected narrative.
